articles.title: Claude Code Automated Refactoring Pipelines in 2026: Running AST Transforms and Letting the Agent Verify Its Own Output
articles.description: Build refactoring pipelines that run TypeScript AST transforms through Claude Code and verify themselves with linters, type-checkers, and test suites before human review.
articles.body_html:
Claude Code Automated Refactoring Pipelines in 2026: Running AST Transforms and Letting the Agent Verify Its Own Output

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Manual refactoring across dozens of files drains velocity. Developers search for patterns, rename exports, update imports, verify linters pass, check types, run tests, and repeat. The latency stacks with every file. Claude Code closes this loop by running the transform, checking the result, fixing errors autonomously, and presenting verified output.

The difference: instead of dictating edits line by line, engineers give Claude a verifiable criterion (tests pass, types check, lint succeeds) and let the agent retry until the check returns green. The manual search-replace-verify cycle becomes a single prompt with machine-confirmed correctness.

Problem flowchart showing manual refactor workflow with failure points

Solution flowchart showing autonomous refactor pipeline with self-verification

Key Takeaways

  • Claude Code verifies its own refactors by running linters, type-checkers, and test suites autonomously before stopping.
  • Stop hooks enforce mechanical checks (like tsc --noEmit) at the agent layer, blocking completion until code passes or retry cap is reached.
  • AST transforms using TypeScript Compiler API let Claude execute deterministic rewrites that surface type errors immediately.
  • The Ralph Wiggum pattern loops prompts back to the agent with error output until success criteria pass, turning test failures into repair instructions.
  • Circuit breakers detect infinite retry loops by checking for repeated identical errors and exit after a configurable threshold.

The Verification-First Architecture: Building Refactors That Check Themselves

Claude Code stops when work appears finished. Developers who rely on "looks done" become the test suite. Every mistake sits unnoticed until manual review. Verification-first design gives Claude objective success criteria it evaluates without human intervention.

The architecture separates the transform from its proof. The transform rewrites code using an AST visitor. The proof runs a command (npm test, tsc --noEmit, eslint src/) and parses the exit code. Claude sees the proof output, iterates on failures, and stops only when the command exits zero.

Anthropic's best practices guide puts verification near the top of its workflow recommendations. The guidance: give Claude something it can run that returns pass or fail. Once the agent has that check, it closes the loop without waiting for a developer to notice broken imports.

Concept diagram showing verification-first architecture with separate transform and proof phases

The proof runs in the same session that made the edits. Claude reads compiler output, parses the error messages, and applies fixes in the next iteration. Test failures become repair instructions.

Teams ship this architecture three ways. The first is a prompt that explicitly asks for verification: "rename every export in src/api/ from async function to export const arrow functions and keep going until tsc exits zero". Claude decides when it is satisfied.

The second is a goal: /goal all files in src/api type-check and lint is clean. A separate model checks the conversation after every turn. If the goal is not met, Claude continues. This matters for background runs where the agent sometimes ends a turn with a progress summary before all items resolve.

The third is a Stop hook. The hook script runs whenever Claude tries to end its turn. If the script exits with code 2, Claude Code sends the agent back to work. The enforcement is mechanical and survives session restarts.

AST Transforms With TypeScript Compiler API: What Claude Can Actually Run

TypeScript Compiler API exposes the same AST TypeScript itself parses. Claude writes a visitor that walks the syntax tree, identifies nodes matching a pattern, and emits replacements. The compiler's type-checker surfaces errors immediately after the transform runs.

The workflow: Claude creates a script that uses ts-morph or the native compiler API to load a project, walk declarations, apply a transformation, and save files. The script runs with Node. TypeScript re-checks the edited source and reports broken references.

Here is a transform that renames all named exports to default exports and updates their import statements. The script loads the TypeScript project, finds every file with named exports, replaces export declarations, searches for files importing those names, and rewrites the import syntax.

import { Project, SyntaxKind, ExportDeclaration } from 'ts-morph';

const project = new Project({
  tsConfigFilePath: './tsconfig.json',
});

const sourceFiles = project.getSourceFiles('src/**/*.ts');

for (const file of sourceFiles) {
  const namedExports = file
    .getDescendantsOfKind(SyntaxKind.ExportDeclaration)
    .filter((decl) => decl.getNamedExports().length > 0);

  if (namedExports.length === 0) continue;

  const exportName = namedExports[0].getNamedExports()[0].getName();

  // Replace named export with default export
  const exportDecl = file.getExportDeclarations()[0];
  exportDecl.remove();
  file.addExportAssignment({
    isExportEquals: false,
    expression: exportName,
  });

  // Find files importing this named export
  const importers = file
    .getReferencingSourceFiles()
    .flatMap((f) => f.getImportDeclarations());

  for (const importDecl of importers) {
    const namedImport = importDecl.getNamedImports().find((n) => n.getName() === exportName);
    if (!namedImport) continue;

    importDecl.setDefaultImport(exportName);
    namedImport.remove();
  }

  file.saveSync();
}

console.log('Refactor complete. Run tsc to verify.');

The script rewrites declarations and updates every import that referenced the old name. TypeScript Compiler API tracks references automatically. The agent never manually searches for import statements.

After the transform runs, Claude executes tsc --noEmit to surface type errors. If broken imports remain, the compiler lists them. Claude reads the output, identifies files with errors, and applies fixes in the next iteration.

The TypeScript 5.7 release notes document the ts-morph integration and confirm that getReferencingSourceFiles() returns every file with an import or type reference to the target. The return value includes dynamic imports and type-only imports, so the visitor catches edge cases manual search-replace misses.

AST transform workflow showing code manipulation and verification

The Ralph Wiggum Loop: Autonomous Retry Until Tests Pass

The Ralph Wiggum pattern loops a prompt back to the agent with error output until success criteria pass. The pattern emerged in mid-2025 and became standard for autonomous refactors by early 2026. Instead of one-shot prompts, the loop intercepts Claude's stop attempt, checks whether criteria are met, and re-feeds error messages if the check fails.

The implementation: a wrapper script runs Claude in a subprocess, captures the session output, checks whether the target test suite passes, and restarts Claude with the test failure as a new prompt if the suite exits non-zero.

import { spawn } from 'child_process';
import { readFileSync, writeFileSync } from 'fs';

interface RetryConfig {
  maxRetries: number;
  verifyCommand: string;
  initialPrompt: string;
}

async function ralphWiggumLoop(config: RetryConfig): Promise<void> {
  let attempt = 0;
  let lastError = '';

  while (attempt < config.maxRetries) {
    const prompt = attempt === 0 ? config.initialPrompt : `Previous attempt failed:\n${lastError}\n\nFix the errors and try again.`;

    const claudeProcess = spawn('claude', ['-p', prompt], {
      stdio: ['pipe', 'pipe', 'pipe'],
    });

    await new Promise<void>((resolve) => {
      claudeProcess.on('close', () => resolve());
    });

    // Run verification
    const verifyProcess = spawn('sh', ['-c', config.verifyCommand], {
      stdio: ['pipe', 'pipe', 'pipe'],
    });

    const verifyOutput: string[] = [];
    verifyProcess.stderr.on('data', (chunk) => verifyOutput.push(chunk.toString()));

    const exitCode = await new Promise<number>((resolve) => {
      verifyProcess.on('close', (code) => resolve(code ?? 1));
    });

    if (exitCode === 0) {
      console.log('Verification passed. Refactor complete.');
      return;
    }

    lastError = verifyOutput.join('');
    attempt++;
  }

  throw new Error(`Refactor failed after ${config.maxRetries} attempts.`);
}

ralphWiggumLoop({
  maxRetries: 8,
  verifyCommand: 'npm test 2>&1',
  initialPrompt: 'Refactor all API handlers to use async/await and ensure tests pass.',
});

The loop runs Claude in programmatic mode (-p) with piped output. After Claude finishes, the script runs the verification command and captures stderr. If the command exits non-zero, the loop restarts Claude with the error output appended to the prompt.

Ralph Wiggum loop execution flow showing retry mechanism with error feedback

The verification command can be any executable that returns zero on success. Test suites, linters, type-checkers, and custom validation scripts all work. The loop does not parse the output format. It feeds the raw error text back to Claude and lets the model interpret the failure.

The retry cap prevents infinite loops when the agent repeatedly applies the same broken fix. The default is eight attempts, matching Claude Code's built-in Stop hook block limit. If the loop exhausts retries without passing verification, it throws an error with the last failure message.

Teams running Ralph Wiggum loops in CI often set maxRetries to three and treat exhaustion as a build failure. The agent either fixes the issue in three tries or the pipeline alerts a human. No one watches the loop run.

Real Pipeline: Rename Exports Across 50 Files, Let the Agent Fix Broken Imports

A production refactor at a team supporting 200 microservices renamed barrel exports in 50 shared utility files. The old convention exported everything from an index file. The new convention used named files. The agent ran the rename, TypeScript reported 180 broken import paths, and Claude fixed every one autonomously.

The prompt: "Rename every file in packages/utils/src/ to match the export it contains and update all imports across the monorepo. Keep going until tsc exits zero and pnpm test passes."

Claude created an AST script using ts-morph that iterated each utility file, extracted the primary export name, renamed the file, and updated the barrel index. The script ran and committed the renames. TypeScript reported errors in 180 files importing the old paths.

The agent read the type-checker output, identified the import statements causing errors, and applied fixes. Some imports used type-only syntax (import type). Others aliased the imported name. Claude handled both cases. After fixing imports, the agent ran tests. Three test files imported utilities with hardcoded relative paths instead of the package name. Claude updated those imports and re-ran the suite.

The entire process took 11 minutes. No human intervention between the prompt and the verified result. The final output included a commit message listing every renamed file and a summary of import updates.

The key: TypeScript's error messages are deterministic. The compiler lists the exact file, line, and expected import path. Claude parses that output directly. No heuristics or fuzzy matching. The fix is mechanical.

For related automation patterns with batch edits, see Claude Code MultiEdit: Write Batch Refactors. For AST-driven workflows in general, see AI-Powered TypeScript Refactoring Workflows.

Large-scale refactor verification with automated error correction

Verification Hooks: Linting, Type-Checking, and Test Runs Before Human Review

Stop hooks enforce mechanical checks before Claude ends a turn. The hook runs every time Claude attempts to stop. If the hook script exits with code 2, Claude Code sends the agent back to work with the hook's stderr output as the reason.

The hook definition sits in .claude/settings.json. The example below runs TypeScript's type-checker and blocks the stop if any errors remain.

{
  "hooks": {
    "Stop": [
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "pnpm tsc --noEmit 1>&2 || exit 2"
      }
    ]
  }
}

The command redirects stdout to stderr so Claude receives compiler output as the blocking reason. The || exit 2 clause ensures the hook exits with code 2 when tsc finds errors. Without that clause, the hook would exit with tsc's exit code, and Claude Code treats any non-zero exit as a block.

Teams layer multiple checks. This configuration runs linting, type-checking, and unit tests in sequence.

{
  "hooks": {
    "Stop": [
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "pnpm eslint src/ 1>&2 || exit 2"
      },
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "pnpm tsc --noEmit 1>&2 || exit 2"
      },
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "pnpm test --run 1>&2 || exit 2"
      }
    ]
  }
}

Each hook runs in order. If any hook exits 2, the remaining hooks do not run and Claude receives the error output from the first failure. The agent applies a fix and attempts to stop again. The hooks re-run with the updated code.

Stop hooks execution flow showing sequential verification gates

Stop hooks are enforced by the harness, not by the prompt. The agent cannot decide to skip them. If the hook blocks eight stops in a row with no tool call between attempts, Claude Code overrides the next block and ends the turn. The cap prevents infinite loops when the agent repeatedly applies a fix that does not resolve the error.

The cap is configurable via CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP environment variable. The default is eight. Teams running refactors with complex multi-file dependencies raise the cap to 15 or 20. Setting it too high risks wasting tokens on futile retries.

The official documentation confirms that Stop hooks run after every stop attempt and that code 2 is the only exit code that blocks completion while sending feedback to the agent. Code 1 logs a warning but allows the stop to proceed.

When the Agent Gets Stuck: Detecting Infinite Loops and Adding Circuit Breakers

Agents retry the same broken fix when verification output is ambiguous or when the agent misinterprets the error. Circuit breakers detect repeated identical failures and exit before exhausting the retry budget.

The simplest circuit breaker tracks error message hashes. After each verification failure, the breaker hashes the error output and checks whether the hash appeared in the last three attempts. If the same error repeats three times, the breaker exits with a detailed log showing what Claude kept trying.

import { createHash } from 'crypto';

interface CircuitState {
  errorHashes: string[];
  maxRepeats: number;
}

function hashError(output: string): string {
  return createHash('sha256').update(output).digest('hex').slice(0, 16);
}

function checkCircuit(state: CircuitState, errorOutput: string): boolean {
  const hash = hashError(errorOutput);
  state.errorHashes.push(hash);

  if (state.errorHashes.length < state.maxRepeats) {
    return false;
  }

  const recent = state.errorHashes.slice(-state.maxRepeats);
  const allSame = recent.every((h) => h === hash);

  if (allSame) {
    console.error(`Circuit breaker tripped: same error repeated ${state.maxRepeats} times.`);
    console.error(`Last error:\n${errorOutput}`);
    return true;
  }

  return false;
}

// Usage in retry loop
const circuit: CircuitState = { errorHashes: [], maxRepeats: 3 };

while (attempt < maxRetries) {
  // ... run Claude and verification ...

  if (exitCode !== 0) {
    if (checkCircuit(circuit, verifyOutput)) {
      throw new Error('Circuit breaker: infinite loop detected.');
    }
    lastError = verifyOutput;
    attempt++;
  }
}

The hash is 16 hex characters, enough to distinguish unique errors without storing full text. The breaker checks only the last N attempts rather than the entire history. This prevents early errors from triggering the breaker after the agent makes progress.

Circuit breaker concept showing infinite loop detection mechanism

The breaker saves time and tokens. Without it, an agent stuck on the same error consumes the full retry budget before failing. With it, the loop exits after three identical attempts and surfaces the problem immediately.

A more sophisticated circuit breaker parses structured error formats. TypeScript errors include file paths, line numbers, and error codes. The breaker extracts those fields and checks whether the same file and line repeat. If the agent keeps breaking the same import three times, the breaker exits even if the error message text varies slightly.

For CI integration patterns that use these techniques, see Claude Code CI: Agentic Review, Test, and Auto-Fix.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Claude Code support AST transforms out of the box?

No. Claude Code provides file operations, shell execution, and code intelligence tools but does not include native AST transform APIs. Developers write Node scripts that use ts-morph or TypeScript Compiler API directly, and Claude runs those scripts via the shell execution tool.

How does a Stop hook differ from a prompt that asks for verification?

A Stop hook is enforced by Claude Code (the harness) and runs every time the agent attempts to end its turn, regardless of whether the agent remembered to verify. A prompt-based check relies on the agent's reasoning and may be skipped if the agent decides the work is complete.

What happens if Stop hooks block 50 times in a row?

Claude Code caps hook blocks at eight by default (configurable via CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP). After eight consecutive blocks with no tool call between attempts, Claude Code overrides the next block and allows the turn to end. The cap prevents infinite loops from exhausting token budgets.

Can verification commands include external API calls?

Yes. The verification command is any shell command that exits zero on success. Teams run commands that call REST endpoints, check deployment status, or validate live systems. The command output returns to Claude as feedback.

How do circuit breakers interact with Stop hooks?

Circuit breakers sit in the wrapper script that calls Claude Code, not in the hooks themselves. The breaker checks verification output after each Claude run. If the breaker detects a repeated error, it exits the wrapper script before invoking Claude again. Stop hooks continue running within each individual Claude session.

Conclusion

Refactoring pipelines that verify themselves eliminate the latency between edit and confirmation. Claude Code runs the transform, checks the result, fixes errors autonomously, and presents verified output. The loop closes without human review until mechanical checks pass. Stop hooks enforce those checks at the agent layer. Circuit breakers detect futile retries and exit before exhausting token budgets. The architecture separates the transform from its proof and lets the compiler, linter, and test suite decide when the work is complete.

Imagine walking into your favourite little café on a rainy afternoon.

You're deciding what to order, and your brain runs through a quick checklist.

  • Is it cold outside AND am I sleepy? → Hot matcha latte.🍵
  • Am I hungry OR did I skip lunch? → Add a strawberry croissant.🥐
  • Is there NO decaf left? → Guess I'm having tea instead.☕

Congratulations. You just acted like a computer processor.

When we write software, whether it's an API, a mobile app, or an AI model, it feels abstract, almost magical. Lines of code appear on a screen, buttons respond, and data flows around the world.

Underneath all of that, though, a computer doesn't understand JavaScript, Python, or English.

It only understands electrical signals: ON or OFF. High voltage or low voltage. 1 or 0.

And the tiny decision makers that turn those 1s and 0s into actual logic? Those are logic gates.

Grab a warm drink, open your notebook, and let's see how the simplest rules in electronics quietly build the entire digital world. 🧋

01. What Actually Is a Logic Gate?

Think of a logic gate as a tiny, stubborn gatekeeper sitting on an electrical circuit.

It takes one or more binary inputs (0s and 1s), applies one simple rule, and produces a single binary output (0 or 1).

No guessing. No "maybe." Just clean, predictable cause and effect.

In physical hardware, modern logic gates are built using microscopic transistors acting like ultra fast electronic switches. Billions of them packed onto a single chip.

You don't need an electrical engineering degree to understand how they think. You just need to know the rules each gate follows.

02. The Core Trio: AND, OR, and NOT

Almost every logical decision starts with three basic building blocks.

1. The AND Gate (Both Must Be True)

An AND gate is strict. It only outputs 1 when EVERY input is 1.

- 0 AND 0 → 0
- 0 AND 1 → 0
- 1 AND 0 → 0
- 1 AND 1 → 1

Think of a vault that requires two keys turned at the exact same time. One key isn't enough. Both have to be present.

In everyday code, this is the exact same idea behind.

if (isLoggedIn && hasPermission) { ... }

2. The OR Gate (At Least One Is True)

An OR gate is much more relaxed. ** It outputs 1 if AT LEAST ONE input is 1.**
- 0 OR 0 → 0
- 0 OR 1 → 1
- 1 OR 0 → 1
- 1 OR 1 → 1

Think of unlocking your front door using either your house key OR a smart passcode. Either option gets you inside.

In code,

if (isAdmin || isEditor) { ... }

3. The NOT Gate (The Plot Twist)

A NOT gate (also called an inverter) only takes one input and flips it.
- NOT 0 → 1
- NOT 1 → 0

If the signal is ON, it turns it OFF. If it's OFF, it turns it ON.

In code, it's your familiar exclamation mark.

if (!isMaintenanceMode) { ... }

Simple so far, right? Three tiny rules. Nothing intimidating.

03. The Interesting Ones: XOR, NAND, and NOR

Once you get comfortable with AND, OR, and NOT, a few combined gates start showing up everywhere.

The XOR Gate (Exclusive OR - "One or the Other, Not Both")

An ordinary OR gate says "yes" if both inputs are 1. XOR is pickier. It outputs 1 ONLY when the inputs are different.
- 0 XOR 0 → 0
- 0 XOR 1 → 1
- 1 XOR 0 → 1
- 1 XOR 1 → 0

Think of a café deal. "Choose a free muffin OR a free cookie—not both😏"

XOR turns out to be a superstar in computing. It's used in binary addition, comparing values for equality, error checking, and even basic cryptography.

NAND and NOR (The Flipped Twins)

- NAND is simply AND followed by NOT (it outputs 0 only when all inputs are 1).
- NOR is simply OR followed by NOT (it outputs 1 only when all inputs are 0).

🍓 *NAND Gate (Not Both) * - Think of a power strip with a safety breaker. Everything runs normally until you plug in two heavy appliances at the exact same time. Then it trips and cuts the power off.

🍓 NOR Gate (Neither) - Think of a quiet study room's "Available" sign outside the door. It only lights up green when neither desk inside is occupied. The moment even one person walks in, the light turns off.

Wait, why make gates that just flip AND and OR?

Because in real silicon hardware, NAND and NOR gates are actually simpler and cheaper to build with transistors than AND and OR gates.

04. The Coolest Trick: Universal Gates

Here's a detail that feels like a magic trick the first time you see it.

NAND and NOR are called universal gates.

Why? Because using ONLY NAND gates (or ONLY NOR gates), you can build AND, OR, NOT, XOR, and literally any digital circuit in existence.

- Connect both inputs of a NAND gate together? You just built a NOT gate.
- Put a NOT-style NAND after another NAND? You just built an AND gate.
- Arrange a few more? You have OR and XOR.

That means a manufacturer doesn't need dozens of completely different physical components to build a processor. They can repeat simple, reliable building blocks over and over again at massive scale.

Sometimes the smartest engineering isn't about inventing complicated parts. It's about finding simple parts that compose well.

05. How Tiny Gates Become a Computer

Okay, flipping a few 1s and 0s is neat. But how do we go from that to running an app or rendering graphics?

It happens in layers.

1. Arithmetic (Adders)

Combine an XOR gate and an AND gate, and you get a Half Adder, a circuit that can actually add two binary digits together (1 + 1 = 10 in binary, which is 2!). Chain a few together, and your hardware can do math.

Think of a tally counter with a rollover bell. When you click past its single-digit limit, it resets back to zero and dings a bell to tell the next column over, "Hey, carry one!"

2. Memory (Latches & Flip-Flops)

Feed the output of logic gates back into their own inputs in a clever loop, and suddenly the circuit can hold onto a 1 or a 0 even after the original button press ends. That's the foundation of computer memory.

Think of a physical light switch on your wall compared to a doorbell button. A doorbell only rings while your finger is pressing it, whereas a light switch clicks into place and remembers your choice long after you walk away.

3. Control & Processing (CPUs)

Combine arithmetic circuits, memory registers, and decision logic by the millions, and now your chip can fetch instructions, compare numbers, branch into if/else paths, and run programs billions of times per second.

Every highlevel if statement you write eventually gets translated down into electrical signals racing through pathways of these exact gates.

## 06. Why Software Developers Should Care

You probably won't wire up physical NAND gates while building a frontend form or a REST API. Still, knowing how logic gates behave shows up in surprising places:

- Boolean logic & cleaner conditions: Understanding equivalence rules (like De Morgan's Laws—turning `!(isReady && isValid)` into `!isReady || !isValid`) helps untangle messy `if` statements.
- Short-circuit evaluation: When you write `user && user.profile`, JavaScript uses the exact nature of AND logic—if the first side is false, there's no point checking the second.
- Bitwise flags & permissions: Systems often pack multiple true/false settings into a single number using bitwise `&` (AND), `|` (OR), and `^` (XOR) because hardware handles them in a single heartbeat.
- Systems thinking: Logic gates are the ultimate reminder that reliable, complex systems are built out of small, predictable pieces with crystal-clear rules.

A Little Takeaway Before We Go 🍓

When you look at a modern laptop or smartphone, it's easy to think of it as impossibly complicated.

And at full scale, it is.

Yet at its very core, everything comes down to billions of tiny switches quietly asking simple questions.
- Are both of these ON?
- Is at least one of these ON?
- Should I flip this signal?

One tiny yes or no at a time, stacked together into something extraordinary.

Next time you write an if (a && b) in your code, take a second to appreciate the millions of microscopic gates underneath making sure that simple question gets answered in a fraction of a nanosecond.

Until the next cup of code. ☕

🍓 Strawberry Tech Notes - learning the details behind the code.

articles.body_html:
OpenAI plans to retire /v1/prompts on November 30, 2026. Here's the uncomfortable truth: publishing a shutdown date proves nothing about customer safety. Without verified dependencies and explicit exit criteria, API retirement can become a production incident.

Why Application Modernization Services Need Retirement Proof

Removing /v1 is easy. Proving that no production workflow depends on it is hard.

For engineering teams evaluating software product modernization services, the deliverable should be an evidence-backed retirement decision, not a dashboard showing declining request counts.

Zero observed traffic does not prove zero dependency.

A quarterly billing process, dormant integration, or disaster-recovery script may remain invisible for weeks.

What Proves a Legacy API Is Safe to Retire?

A legacy API is safe to retire when every material consumer is identified or formally risk-assessed, replacements pass production-relevant contract tests, migration is verified, and residual calls are explained. The observation window must include infrequent jobs. Engineering, product, and security must approve the cutover, with monitoring and a tested recovery plan in place.

Build a Dependency Inventory That Catches Invisible Clients

Start with API gateway logs. Then reconcile the findings against:

  • OAuth clients, API keys, and service accounts.
  • Repository searches and infrastructure configurations.
  • Webhooks, message queues, and scheduled jobs.
  • Customer integrations and partner contracts.
  • AI agents, MCP tools, and internal automation.
  • Disaster-recovery and batch-processing workflows.

What Belongs in a Complete API Dependency Inventory?

An actionable dependency inventory records the consumer or tenant, accountable owner, endpoint and version, authentication identity, last-seen production request, call frequency, business function, schedule, replacement, migration status, and evidence link. It also includes non-HTTP dependencies such as webhooks, message queues, batch exports, and AI agents invoking tools. Unknown owners are open risks, not completed rows.

Query Real Consumers, Not Aggregate Traffic

Use a gateway-log query to identify active callers:

SELECT consumer_id,
       COUNT(*) AS calls,
       MAX(request_time) AS last_seen
FROM api_gateway_logs
WHERE api_version = 'v1'
  AND environment = 'production'
  AND request_time >= NOW() - INTERVAL '90 days'
GROUP BY consumer_id
ORDER BY last_seen DESC;

This PostgreSQL-style query provides a starting point, not retirement approval.

A 90-day window may miss annual reconciliations, inactive partner integrations, or emergency recovery operations.

Compare observed requests with known business schedules.

Consumer Dependency Migration status
Billing worker Nightly /v1/invoices Migrating
Partner A Quarterly /v1/export Hold
Internal dashboard /v1/metrics Verified

Illustrative example. Production inventories require owners, evidence links, and last-seen timestamps.

Important: Migrating 99% of request volume means little if the remaining 1% belongs to a critical enterprise customer.

Quokka Labs Service Retirement Worksheet: Seven Exit Gates

A retirement worksheet turns assumptions into verifiable engineering decisions.

Copy this template into an architecture decision record, Jira ticket, or GitHub pull request. Attach timestamped evidence to every gate.

Exit gate Required evidence Decision
Consumer coverage 100% of known critical consumers have identified owners; unknown critical identities resolved Pass / Hold
Functional parity Authentication, schemas, errors, retries, pagination, and idempotency tested Pass / Hold
Migration verification Critical consumers demonstrate successful replacement usage in production Pass / Hold
Traffic validation Zero unexplained legacy calls across a complete business cycle plus buffer Pass / Hold
Security and compliance Credential revocation, audit retention, and data obligations documented Pass / Hold
Operational recovery Alerts, accountable responders, and tested rollback or recovery procedures Pass / Hold
Final authorization Engineering, product, and security approvals recorded with evidence Pass / Hold

Decision rule: Any unresolved critical dependency means NO-GO.

An exception requires a named decision-maker, documented business impact, and an approved mitigation.

Which Exit Criteria Should Block an API Shutdown?

Block retirement if a critical consumer has no owner, migration lacks production evidence, replacement behavior differs on important edge cases, or infrequent workflows remain untested. Also block when remaining calls cannot be attributed, compliance obligations are unclear, or the team cannot detect and recover from cutover failures. A calendar deadline never overrides a failed safety gate.

Execute a Controlled, Recoverable API Retirement

Step 1: Publish a Migration Contract

Document old-to-new endpoint mappings, changed fields, authentication requirements, error codes, and retry behavior.

For critical integrations, test real business transactions instead of relying exclusively on schema compatibility.

Step 2: Communicate Deprecation Programmatically

Use standardized HTTP response headers:

  • Deprecation — RFC 9745 communicates deprecation timing.
  • Sunset — RFC 8594 communicates when an endpoint is expected to become unavailable.

Also notify identified consumers directly and provide migration documentation.

These headers communicate lifecycle changes; they do not prove migration is complete.

Step 3: Migrate Consumers in Controlled Groups

Move approved consumer groups to the replacement API.

Track:

  • Production migration completion by consumer.
  • HTTP 4xx/5xx rates and latency.
  • Missing webhooks or message events.
  • Business transaction success rates.
  • Unexpected legacy requests.

Stop migration when material regressions occur.

Step 4: Enforce the Go/No-Go Decision

Disable legacy routing only after every mandatory exit gate passes.

When appropriate, return 410 Gone with a stable migration link for permanently retired endpoints.

Preserve monitoring after the shutdown.

Step 5: Archive the Retirement Evidence

Retain dependency inventories, test results, stakeholder approvals, customer notices, and operational records according to company policy.

For broader architecture decisions, explore Quokka Labs' AI-powered legacy modernization strategy, which explains how to assess, refactor, replace, or retire aging systems through controlled migration.

Where Application Modernization Services Reduce Retirement Risk

Retiring an API does not always mean replacing the entire application.

Some systems require API decoupling, others need data migration, and certain workloads can remain operational behind a compatibility layer.

Quokka Labs' application modernization services support phased migration, legacy integration, and application restructuring while protecting operational continuity.

The objective is to eliminate unsupported dependencies without disrupting workflows customers still rely on.

FAQ: Legacy API Retirement

Is 30 Days of Zero Traffic Enough?

No. The observation window must cover the longest legitimate consumption cycle. Quarterly exports, seasonal workloads, and disaster-recovery processes may remain invisible in short monitoring periods.

What Is the Difference Between API Deprecation and Retirement?

Deprecation announces that an API should no longer be used.

Retirement ends its operational availability.

Under RFC 9745, deprecation signaling does not itself change how a resource behaves.

Who Approves a Legacy API Retirement?

Engineering verifies technical readiness. Product evaluates customer impact. Security and compliance review controls.

A designated accountable owner makes the final decision and records any accepted exceptions.

Final Takeaway: Retire Dependencies, Not Just Endpoints

A successful API retirement is not measured by deleted code. It is measured by verified migrations, preserved business operations, and documented risk decisions.

Drawing on its stated 15+ years of product engineering experience, Quokka Labs helps organizations evaluate complex application architectures and plan controlled modernization.

Its software product modernization services help engineering teams turn hidden dependencies into actionable migration plans.

Planning to retire a legacy API?

Connect with Quokka Labs to discuss dependency discovery, modernization architecture, and production cutover readiness.

Dev discussion: What's the most unexpected dependency you've discovered during an API retirement: a scheduled job, a partner integration, or an undocumented internal client?

articles.body_html:
This is the last part of a series on building an HL7 v2-to-FHIR R4 interoperability service in public. The repository is ND-codes/nhs-interop-platform, and the code as it stood for this article is tagged part-7.

If you are new here, the short version. Many hospital systems send patient events as HL7 version 2, an older plain-text format. National NHS services are moving to FHIR, a newer web format. Something in between has to translate each message, check the patient against national records, and tell someone when it breaks. This repository is a small, working version of that layer. It runs on a laptop with synthetic test data, and you can fork it and follow along.

I built this with Claude Code, and said so in Parts 4, 5 and 6. This part is the accounting.

Most writing about AI and code argues from impressions. I have seven weeks of dated evidence instead: every defect in this project, and how each one was actually found. The answer turned out to be more specific than "it helps with boilerplate" and more useful than "always review the output".

The accounting

Sorting every defect by discovery route.

Found by reading the code against a specific question

A Terraform default_tags block that was commented out while the compliance documentation described its benefit in the present tense. Four NHS numbers in pds-client log lines, plus the same identifier used as an outbound X-Request-ID. A cygpath call that scoped make test to Git Bash on Windows. make integration installing into a PEP 668 interpreter. A terraform.tfvars.example the quickstart told you to copy and which did not exist. Eight runbook links that had never resolved. Ten false claims in
docs/security.md and four more in docs/architecture.md. The complete absence of any S3 client in a project whose compliance table cited an S3 lifecycle rule as its retention control.

That is a long list, and it is the strongest mode. Reading forty files and checking whether each cited thing exists is tedious, mechanical, and exactly the work that gets skipped at the end of a week. Most of Parts 5 and 6 came from one question each: which rows of this document are false, and which steps of this quickstart fail on a machine that is not mine.

Found by running the system

The circuit breaker gauge that no service exported, found by starting
transform and reading /metrics instead of reading the code. A timing claim about for: 2m against a 30-second reset_timeout that turned out to be wrong when measured. A fuzzing run over 28,000 mutated messages confirming no patient value reached an exception message.

Found by me running the real thing

The longest list, and the one that matters.

The PDS circuit breaker was applied as a decorator to a coroutine function. pybreaker counted the returned coroutine object as a success, the real failure raised later on await, outside the breaker, and the breaker never opened. The fix Part 4 shipped for an alert that could never fire therefore still could not fire. The test passed because it drove the breaker synchronously.

A dead-letter volume owned by root while the container runs as uid 10001, so every dead-letter write failed with PermissionError, and the message was lost.

hl7_dlq_oldest_seconds set only when pruning ran, so it froze below its own threshold and the alert built to watch it could never fire.

A raw | in a FHIR query, which RFC 3986 does not permit in a query and Tomcat rejects with a 400 that curl -sf then swallowed, so the walkthrough reported a missing Patient that was there.

Two zlib CVEs that broke every image job until the base stage applied Debian security updates.

And then alerts actually reached a person. IngestNoTraffic emailed me six times in two days about a demo stack nobody was using, which is the rule doing its job on a stack left idle. None of the alerts ever told me they were over, because send_resolved defaults to false for email_configs, so from an inbox an incident that has ended looks exactly like one still running.

Found by readers

Kevin Mayfield on CHI numbers arriving in the NHS Number field, and on the number changing when a patient moves between the Scottish and English NHS, which makes keying patient identity on it unsafe. Mustafa Erbay on PV1-19 for encounter identity. Readers of Part 1 on conditional update against conditional create, the PID-8 concept map, partial birth dates, PID-3 assigning authorities. Nan on the alerts reaching nobody. Amorizz and upordown.online on the absence of absent() and up alerts, which became most of this week's code. Kartik on make break-pds not running in CI. Paul Lovelace on whether make walkthrough ran in CI. It did not. It does now.

Found by the assistant's own tests, before shipping

One. A pybreaker listener reading new_state.state where the attribute is new_state.name. getattr with a default does not raise, so the gauge would have sat at zero while the breaker was open: a fix leaving the alert unfireable while adding a green dashboard panel.

One, out of all of them.

A mistake in the other direction

Part 6 said make restore-pds left the alert firing and the script should be fixed to send traffic. It already sent traffic, and had since Part 4. The assistant described the script from what the dashboard showed, without reading it, and I published that. Running the full script again this week closed the breaker in under a minute. Part 6 now carries a correction.

And one that nearly shipped this week. The first draft of this part's code quieted those overnight emails by only alerting if traffic had arrived in the last 24 hours. It read well and passed its tests. Evaluated against my live stack while it sat idle, it fired anyway, because the demo had carried traffic earlier that day. Worse, it would have gone silent once an outage passed a day.
It was dropped, and two tests now hold that line.

So the lesson is not "running beats reading". Each catches what the other misses, and skipping either one is how a wrong claim gets out.

The one that belongs on its own

In Part 5 I had the assistant fix a patient identifier leak. It wrote eight tests asserting the NHS number never reaches stdout, deliberately asserting against the formatter's serialised output rather than the log record, because the defect lived in serialisation and caplog would have passed.

Good tests. They covered pds-client, the service being edited.

The identical leak existed in transform, through a completely different mechanism. transform logs str(exc) when a PDS lookup fails, and a HTTPStatusError builds its message from the request URL, and the URL is PDS_CLIENT_URL/<nhs_number>. Every failed lookup logged the patient identifier.

I found it by running a real PDS failure rather than the connection error the tests used, whose message contains no URL. The fix is
services/transform/tests/test_pds_privacy.py.

The tests had been shaped around the instance that was found, not the property that was claimed. The claim was "the NHS number never reaches our logs". What was tested was "these four call sites no longer pass it in extra". Those look the same from inside the diff and are not the same thing at all.

The pattern

Look again at the deepest problems in this project. An S3 bucket with perfect retention controls that nothing writes to. An alert rule watching a metric no service exports. A runbook link pointing at an anchor that was never created. An Alertmanager configuration with no Alertmanager. A retention window with no measurement. A resolution email that never sends.

Every one of them is absence-shaped. And from inside the repository, absence looks exactly like everything being fine. There is no red line in a diff for a file that does not exist, no failing test for a notification nobody receives, no warning for a rule whose series was never created. The code reads correctly because the code is correct. What is missing is the part that would have made it matter.

Reading did find some of them, and the way it found them is the useful part. The empty bucket came to light because the security table cited a lifecycle rule, so there was something to check: what writes to this bucket? The dead runbook links came to light because each alert named an anchor, so there was something to check: does it resolve? Reading finds a missing thing when a document points at where it should be.

When nothing written down names the missing thing, reading has nothing to check against. No file said "an Alertmanager runs here", so no amount of reading noticed there was not one. That was found by a person asking who gets told. The unexported gauge was found by starting the service and looking.

An assistant reads. It reads very well and very patiently, and it has no inbox and no on-call rotation. It notices a missing thing when a document points at it. It cannot notice that nothing arrived.

That is not a limitation you fix with a better prompt. It is a consequence of where the thing sits. It does suggest a cheap habit, though: write down what should exist, so reading has something to check.

What that changed in the code

Three parts of this repository exist because of that pattern, and they are the parts most worth copying.

make walkthrough runs the documented tour as eight assertions and stops on the first step that does not hold. Since this week it runs in CI on every pull request, starting all nine services from nothing, so the quickstart and the behaviour cannot drift apart quietly. A failed check now says which HTTP status it got, so the Part 6 bug would have reported itself in two seconds rather than hiding behind a thirty-second wait.

scripts/break-pds.sh and scripts/break-fhir.sh drive real failures on purpose. An alert proved only by a unit test is not proved. Those scripts found the root-owned dead-letter volume in their first week.

And this week's change, which is the general case. Every alert in this repository watched a rate, a ratio or a gauge. All of them share one blind spot: a service that is down exports none of those, so the rules testing for too much of something go quiet precisely when things are worst. There are now three rules that watch for absence:

- alert: ServiceTargetMissing
  expr: |
    absent(up{job="ingest"})
    or absent(up{job="transform"})
    or absent(up{job="pds-client"})

- alert: BreakerMetricAbsent
  expr: absent(pybreaker_state{name="pds"})

The second is the literal guard against the Part 4 defect recurring.
PDSCircuitOpen watched pybreaker_state for two months while nothing exported it, and a rule that cannot fire is indistinguishable from a rule that is never needed. If that gauge disappears again, something says so.

A useful detail: given a selector, absent() derives the output labels from that selector, so the alert names the missing job without any templating. That only holds for a selector argument; wrap it in an aggregation and the labels are gone. I confirmed the selector behaviour with promtool rather than assuming it, after a test failed on exactly that point. There are twenty promtool cases behind these now, including one asserting that a fully healthy stack fires nothing at all, which matters because a false alarm on a working system is worse than no alarm.

Where it genuinely helped

I want to be as specific about this as about the failures, because "AI is bad at X" is as lazy as the marketing.

The sweep is real, and it is worth a lot. Checking every row of a control table against the filesystem, every documented command against what the Makefile does, every external claim against the primary source. That is work I would not have done by hand, and skipping it is how the documentation got into the state Part 5 found.

Verification against primary sources, when you insist on it, is reliable. HL7 v2.5.1 escape sequences, the FHIR R4 rules on partial dates and nulls, NHS Modulus 11, Terraform's default_tags syntax, PEP 668, Alertmanager's send_resolved defaults: all checked against the specification rather than recalled. That rule exists because of a specific failure, a Trivy flag in Part 2 taken from memory, that broke CI and that I had to fix.

Writing a test that fails against the previous commit before it passes against the new one is a discipline it will follow consistently once it is the standing rule, and it caught the one defect in the list above that was caught before shipping.

And the writing. Seven articles, the runbook, the security model, this changelog.

What I would tell someone starting

Put the assistant where reading pays and put yourself where running pays. They are different jobs, not different quality levels of the same job.

Make it state what it could not check. The single most useful habit in seven weeks was a standing rule that any unverifiable claim gets said out loud rather than hedged into the prose. That is how docs/security.md ended up with a "Claimed, not built" section instead of a table of confident sentences.

Be suspicious of a test written in the same pass as the fix. It will encode the shape of the bug that was found. Ask separately what property you are claiming, and whether anything tests that property rather than that instance.

Run the thing. Then break it on purpose. Then wait for the email.

If you want to try this yourself

You need Docker and make, about 4 GB free for Docker, and no NHS or cloud account. Everything uses synthetic test data, and the national lookup is stubbed by default.

Fork the repository, then:

make demo
make walkthrough
make break-pds

The first two start nine services and prove each step of the tour works. The third breaks the national patient lookup on purpose. Watch the pipeline keep accepting messages, the alert fire about two minutes later, and the email land in a local inbox at localhost:8025. Then make restore-pds puts it back.

If you are switching careers, into tech or into health tech, that exercise is the one worth being able to explain out loud: what failed, what kept working, who got told, and how you know. Most of the interview questions in Part 6 come down to those four.

Then pick one item from the known limitations in CHANGELOG.md and build it. Authentication on POST /hl7 is a good first one. That is the step from following someone else's project to owning a piece of it.

If you fund or buy health tech

Every finding in this series has a question behind it that you can ask a vendor, and none of them needs you to read code.

  • When did an alert last reach a person, and what did it say? A rule that fires into nothing looks identical to one that works.
  • Which controls in your security document can you show me in the code? Ten of mine could not be shown when I checked.
  • What happens to a message when a system you depend on is down? Where does it wait, and for how long?
  • How do you match a patient whose NHS number changes, or arrives as a Scottish CHI number? Mine does not yet, and says so.

A team that answers those with specifics, including what is not built yet, is telling you more than a feature list can.

The series in numbers

Over a hundred commits and more than thirty pull requests. About half the commits, and most of the pull requests, came during the seven weeks of the series. Ninety-two tests. Twelve alert rules with twenty promtool cases behind them, each with a runbook section whose link now resolves. Seven articles.

Roughly a dozen defects found by readers, which is the number I would most want someone starting a build-in-public series to notice.

What is still not built

POST /hl7 has no authentication. No part of the AWS configuration has ever been applied. The dead-letter path does not survive a pod restart, and the bucket with the correct controls still has nothing writing to it. There is no Alertmanager in the Helm charts, so Kubernetes alert delivery does not exist. Patient identity is keyed on the NHS number alone, which is unsafe for exactly the cases Kevin described.

All of it is in docs/security.md under "Claimed, not built", and in
CHANGELOG.md under the 1.0.0 known limitations. A tool that is good at producing confident prose is a reason to be stricter about that list, not looser.

Sources

  • [Prometheus query functions (https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/functions/), for absent() and its label derivation
  • Alertmanager configuration, for the send_resolved defaults
  • Keep a Changelog 1.1.0
  • PEP 668
  • RFC 3986, section 3.4
  • The alert rules in this article were checked with promtool check rules and exercised with promtool test rules; the Alertmanager configuration with amtool check-config 0.34.1
  • docs/ai-usage.md in the repository holds the same accounting, maintained with the code

Thank you

To everyone who read a part and told me something was wrong: Kevin Mayfield, Mustafa Erbay, Nan, Amorizz, upordown.online, Kartik, Paul Lovelace, and the Part 1 commenters who found the mapping defects. Roughly a dozen real problems in this repository exist in fixed form because somebody asked a question I had thought to ask.

That is the actual finding of this series, and it is not about AI at all. The assistant read the code tirelessly and found what was wrong with it. Running the system found what was broken. Other people found what was missing.

Which of those three is weakest in how you work right now?

This is a personal project. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by NHS England or any NHS organisation. It uses the public PDS FHIR sandbox and synthetic test data only. Views are my own.

articles.description: Laid off in August. 11 full interview processes. Take-home assignments, role plays, presentations,...
articles.body_html:
Laid off in August. 11 full interview processes. Take-home assignments, role plays, presentations, final rounds... and 10 rejections.

Then one offer finally landed. 🎉

I was scrolling r/jobsearch this week and ran into this post by u/BodybuilderSad7036. It blew up with 500+ upvotes in less than a day. I ended up reading the whole thing, plus pretty much every comment underneath it. Honestly? It hit way harder than the usual LinkedIn motivation threads.

If you are job hunting right now, yeah, the market feels pretty cooked. I am a full-stack dev building web and AI apps, and seeing how brutal hiring has gotten lately is honestly the main reason I started putting all my shipped projects and experiments up on taqui.in instead of relying on a plain PDF resume alone.

Before anything else, read this one line OP dropped near the top of the post:

"If that's where you are right now, hear me: it's probably not you. Budgets freeze. Roles disappear overnight. Most of it is out of our hands."

Still, waiting around doesn't pay the bills. So I went through their post, plus two really good tricks they only shared in the comments, and turned it into a practical breakdown you can actually use this week. So Let's Gooooo

1. Stop Applying to Everything (And Go After People, Not Just Postings)

Most people open LinkedIn, search one job title, hit "Easy Apply" 60 times, and wonder why their inbox stays completely silent.

OP did the opposite and got very specific about four things:

  • Search every title in your job family: The exact same job goes by five different names. For OP (post-sales SaaS), that meant implementation, onboarding, CSM, account manager, and consultant. If you are in tech, don't only search "Frontend Developer". Search UI Engineer, Design Engineer, Product Engineer, Web Engineer, and Full Stack too.
  • Pick industries where you already have leverage: OP focused on POS SaaS (restaurants, clubs, hospitality) and bilingual/LATAM markets where their background stood out right away.
  • Don't live only on LinkedIn: LinkedIn works, sure, but everyone is competing in the exact same queue. OP also used niche boards like Built In for SaaS roles.
  • Go after the people, not just the job listing: This part actually got cut off right below the first screenshot, and it might be the best tip in the whole post. OP looked up peers, hiring managers, directors, and even VPs around the role they applied for and messaged them directly. That is literally how they got into the company that gave them the offer.

Someone in the comments asked for their exact outreach trick, and OP's reply was super grounded.

They did not pay for LinkedIn Premium. They sent a normal connection request first. Once the person accepted, they used AI to draft a short DM tailored to that person's role, rewrote it manually so it sounded warm and human, and attached their tailored resume.

Will people ignore you? Definitely. People in the comments even vented about former coworkers saying "sure, send me your resume!" and then completely ghosting them. OP's response to that was simple:

"Some people can be apathetic; others are not. It is always worth knocking on the door."

Okay, You Found the Right Roles. Why Are You Still Getting Ghosted?

Because sending the same generic resume to 50 different job descriptions is basically throwing it into a void. And weirdly enough, letting AI blindly rewrite your resume is almost as bad.

Page 2 fixes that.

2. The "Honest Match" AI Resume Workflow (No Fluff Allowed)

Most people use ChatGPT or Claude backwards. They paste a job description and say "rewrite my resume to match this," and the AI turns them into a "visionary, synergistic 10x ninja." Recruiters spot that fake language in two seconds.

OP's workflow is much smarter:

  1. Start with one Master Resume packed with real numbers and specific results.
  2. Ask AI for an honest match check first. Paste your master resume and the job description into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini, and ask for an unfiltered evaluation. If the match is weak, skip it. You just saved yourself an hour.
  3. Only tailor if it is a real match. Have it generate a tailored resume (and a cover letter if the role asks for one).
  4. Cut the AI BS manually. Delete every inflated buzzword before you hit send. Keep every date, title, and metric 100% defensible because you will be asked about them in the interview.

One more thing from Page 2 that every overthinker needs to hear:

"Years of experience" is a wish list, not a hard rule.

If a job asks for 4 years and you have 3, apply anyway. Put your strongest, most relevant work right at the top and back it up with real numbers. Plenty of people get hired without checking every single box on the posting.

Great, You Landed the Interview. Don't Lose Them in the First 3 Minutes.

You made it past the ATS filter and got the recruiter call. This is where a lot of genuinely strong people accidentally talk themselves out of the next round.

Page 3 is where the offer actually gets won, and it also has the most underrated advice in the entire thread.

3. Fix Your Interview Story + Protect Your Sanity With a "Bridge Job"

Stop Giving a Generic Life Story

Recruiters only need to walk away from that first screen knowing two things:

  1. You understand the role and have a real story for why you want this company.
  2. You can help them hit their goals.

It all starts with "Tell me about yourself." Don't ramble through your whole biography. Connect the dots: where you've been, what you've built or done, and why it leads naturally into this exact job. Practice it out loud until it sounds like a normal conversation instead of a stiff sales pitch.

Once you get to the Hiring Manager interview (the one that actually decides things), answer directly with specific examples and bring thoughtful questions. OP's prep trick here is gold: give AI the JD, ask for likely tough questions, practice your answers out loud, and have AI grade you.

For peer interviews, relax a little. Those are mostly about day-to-day work and team vibe. Ask them what the job is actually like.

Get a Bridge Job. Seriously.

Here is the rough part: you can prep well, nail every interview, and still get rejected. The waiting period between rounds drains your bank account and your head fast.

OP's biggest recommendation is to get a bridge job. Freelance work, contract gigs, part-time work, or a side hustle you already had going.

Without a Bridge Job With a Bridge Job
"Unemployed" gap sitting on your resume Active builder or consultant with steady income
Desperate energy during interviews Real leverage, making it feel like you are choosing them
Refreshing Gmail every 10 minutes Structure and routine that protect your mental health

In the comments, one person mentioned how miserable they felt doing Amazon delivery shifts after 5 rejections in two months, and asked what OP actually did. OP replied that they coached tennis (and added padel) because it was a skill they already had.

Their advice was simple: pick something somewhat meaningful using a skill you already know. Freelance bug fixes, landing pages, tutoring, consulting, whatever keeps money coming in without burning you out.

The Quiet Rule Nobody Talks About

Right at the bottom of Page 3, OP wrote a section that hit home for a ton of commenters:

"Pick one or two people you truly trust and tell them what you're going through. But don't overshare, not even with most of your friends and family. It only feeds your anxiety and brings constant questions like 'any news yet?'"

One commenter pointed out that even close family members can drop weirdly insensitive comments without meaning to. Job hunting is mostly an internal battle with your own confidence. You don't need 15 people asking for weekly status updates while you are already stressed. Keep your circle tiny until the offer letter is signed.

Steal This: The 3-Prompt "OFFER" Kit (Copy and Paste)

Since OP's system relies on using AI to filter, cut fluff, and grade your prep, I turned their exact workflow into 3 prompts you can copy right now.

1. The Honest JD Match Checker (Run Before Applying) 

Act as a brutally honest senior hiring manager. Compare my Master Resume below with this Job Description.
1. Give me an unfiltered match score out of 10.
2. List the exact gaps that might get me auto-rejected.
3. Tell me straight: should I invest time applying to this, or skip it? Do not sugarcoat anything.

[PASTE MASTER RESUME]
[PASTE JOB DESCRIPTION]

2. The Zero-Fluff Resume Tailor 

Rewrite only the summary and top bullet points of my resume to align with this Job Description.
STRICT RULES:
- Do NOT invent skills, fake metrics, or exaggerate my titles.
- Ban all AI buzzwords (no "spearheaded", "synergy", "visionary", "leveraged", "cutting-edge").
- Use plain, sharp language with defensible numbers I can explain in an interview.

[PASTE MASTER RESUME]
[PASTE JOB DESCRIPTION]

3. The Hiring Manager Mock Interview Grader 

You are the Hiring Manager for the role below. Ask me 5 realistic, tough interview questions one by one (starting with "Tell me about yourself" tied to this role).
After each answer I give, grade me out of 10 on clarity, relevance, and proof of impact, and tell me exactly how to tighten my answer before moving to the next question.

[PASTE JOB DESCRIPTION]
[PASTE MY TAILORED RESUME]

Honestly, reading real stories like this beats 99% of the recycled "5 tips to crack FAANG" posts out there. If you are in the middle of the grind right now, drop a comment with how many applications or rounds you are at. And if you found a bridge job or cold-DM tactic that actually worked for you, share it so others reading this can try it too :)

I'm Taqui, a full-stack dev from India building web and AI products.

I write about what I'm learning here and ship my actual projects over at taqui.in.

Feel free to drop by and say hi:)

articles.title: How to Auto-Approve Pull Requests Safely: Testing It on a Real Repo
articles.description: TL;DR   Hello everyone! Today, we can no longer imagine modern application development...
articles.body_html:
TL;DR

Hello everyone! Today, we can no longer imagine modern application development without artificial intelligence. Every day, thanks to GPT or Claude, we write thousands of lines of code.

And AI agents can now do more than just write code. They can work on tasks, make changes in a repository and even open pull requests. It feels a bit like a software factory: you give an agent a task, and it comes back with a PR.

But there is still one step where a person usually has to get involved: someone needs to review and approve that PR. And when agents can create changes much faster, the approval process can become a bottleneck.

So what should you do? Can we automatically approve simple changes without letting every PR through? In this article, I want to test Qodo's approval workflows on a real repository. We'll look at both sides: a PR that can be automatically approved and a PR that should stay with a human reviewer.

Well then, let’s begin! 🏎️

🔎 The idea is simple

Yes, I may be stating the obvious, but using artificial intelligence to check code can help a reviewer spot things they might otherwise miss.

Yes, but you might object to this and say, why would AI need to check what AI has written? Well, an agent can make mistakes too, and the person who gave it the task still needs a way to check the result. Let me give you a simple example: an agent might use class instead of className in JSX.

<div class="myClass"></div>

Depending on your project's configuration, a linter may catch this. But not every issue is as simple as a typo, and a reviewer still has to look at the change and decide what to do with it.

Now let's think about this problem on a larger scale. Whether you work at a company or maintain an open-source project, you may have many PRs coming in from both people and agents. Some are small and routine, while others need a closer look from a person.

So, in the next chapter, I would like to test a way to handle both!

🔗 Integrating AI into the PR review process for a project

Today, it’s as simple as it gets, especially considering how much the industry has evolved recently. There are many companies that provide AI code review services.

In my recent article, I already looked at the popular services available for this purpose and explained why I chose Qodo.

In it, I examined all aspects in detail and compared the services based on what I consider to be the main selection criteria in this field. You can also take a look at it.

In short, Qodo goes beyond ordinary AI code review: it's a Code Governance platform that combines review, standards, cross-repo analysis and agentic workflows in one product.

Once you've set it up for your repository, Qodo can review your PRs. But what happens after that review? Let's find out!

💻 Configuring Policy-Driven Approval on a real repository

Installing Qodo is extremely simple and won’t take much time. Just go to this page and connect the app to your repository.

After that, all that remains is to register on the website. The registration process there is as simple as can be.

After that, you can choose a plan or opt for a trial. I won’t be covering that process in this article; let’s move on to the features.

I set it up on my repository:

✅ Policy-Driven Approval feature

If you’ve worked with tools like these, you know that they simply generate a report on what’s in the code and what could be improved. This is helpful for a reviewer, but a significant gap remains: someone still has to approve the pull request so that a maintainer can merge it. And that’s where things get really interesting.

If you have ever worked on a project or are currently working on one, you’ve probably noticed that the Approve process often repeats itself. As a reviewer, you follow the same verification script, whether you think about it or not.

So, the main idea is that you can define rules for when a PR can be automatically approved. For example, a small change might be a good candidate, while a change in a sensitive part of the project might still need a person to look at it.

It is important to note that an approval is not the same as an auto-merge. Whether a PR can be merged also depends on the repository's settings and other required checks.

🧪 Test 1: a PR that can be automatically approved

If you’ve done everything correctly, then by navigating to the Workflows tab, you’ll see a list of your workflows (what a surprise). Let’s add our first workflow here:

I’ll call it simply "My new workflow", but you can name it whatever you like. Next, I’ll add the conditions under which my pull request will be automatically approved. To do this, I’ll click the Add condition button and set up my own rules for GitHub.

Once configured, simply click the Create workflow button. Note that there is also an active toggle; if enabled, your workflow will immediately begin running for all subsequent pull requests.

Now that our workflow has been created, we can activate it and check whether Qodo is able to approve it.

I will create a simple pull request as a test, adding social media links to the website.

After that, Qodo, which we added earlier, will start working for me, and if everything is fine with the code, it will let me know that it’s ready for merging.

And hurray, our code was approved! But that doesn't mean the PR has been merged or that other repository checks can be ignored.

🗝️ Test 2: keeping a PR with a human reviewer

Okay, but what if a PR shouldn't be automatically approved? This is just as important as the first test. We don't want to set up a workflow that treats every change in the same way.

For the second test, I'll configure a Guard for a case that should require a person to review the PR. Then I'll create another test PR that matches that case.

To begin, let’s create a Guard. To do this, click the Approval guards button:

Now, let’s configure Guard. There are only a few settings, so the whole process takes just about five minutes. You can select the scope for your repositories and, if you wish, specify certain users whose contributions should never be subject to Auto Approve by Qodo, even when the code is perfectly fine. This can be particularly useful when dealing with code generated by an AI bot.

If everything is done correctly, the following will appear:

Now, let’s try applying these changes to the pull request I created earlier. Qodo has approved it, but what happens if I add further changes in a subsequent commit using my own account?

I added the changes (just changed “twitter” to “x”); there’s no error in them. Since I'd added a Guard for my account after the first approval, the new commit triggered a re-check, and the PR now matched the Guard:

Qodo withdrew its approval, even though the code is fine, and that’s because I’ve now configured it so that it no longer happens from my account.

And in the future, my pull requests will no longer be auto-approved. This is a very useful feature, let's say, when configuring it for code generated by bots, or when a new employee joins the company.

And that’s not all! If someone commits an incorrect code, the approval will also be removed, for example.

🏭 Why this matters for a software factory

I was thinking about how this could work in a software factory, where AI agents work on tasks, write code and open pull requests. That's great, but someone still needs to approve those PRs. Approval workflows and Guards can help make that process more manageable:

  • Handle routine PRs: Changes that meet your conditions can be approved automatically.
  • Keep a person involved: Guards can exclude certain contributors from automatic approval, so their PRs need a human reviewer.
  • Apply the same rules: You define the conditions once and use them across matching pull requests.
  • Keep your merge checks: An approval doesn't replace the other checks and requirements configured for your repository.

So, instead of checking every PR in exactly the same way, you can decide which changes need your attention and which ones can follow the rules you've already set.

🖋️ Conclusion

In this article, we tried out Qodo's approval workflows on a real repository. For the first test, I created a simple PR that added social media links to the website, and Qodo approved it based on the workflow conditions.

But automatic approval isn't something I'd want to use for every PR. I sometimes use AI agents to help me write code, and even when the result looks good at first glance, I still want to check what the agent has actually changed. That's why I also configured an Approval Guard for contributions from a specific user.

Of course, the result depends on the rules you configure. An approval also doesn't mean that a PR has been merged or that other required checks have passed. So before relying on a workflow, it's worth testing both the cases you want to approve automatically and the ones you want to keep for a human reviewer.

For me, that's the most interesting part: you can automate some of the routine without giving up control over the changes that you want to review yourself.

  • Qodo Site: https://qodo.ai
  • Qodo Docs: https://docs.qodo.ai
  • Code Review Academy: https://www.qodo.ai/academy
  • Code review tools: https://www.qodo.ai/academy/ai-code-review-tools-comparison-and-benchmarks
