articles.title: My AI memory marked 471 notes as verified. Nothing had verified them.
articles.description: Go and look at whatever your system calls freshness. The last_checked column, the verified_at field,...
articles.body_html:
Go and look at whatever your system calls freshness. The last_checked
column, the verified_at field, the little amber badge that says a record is
still good. Then answer one question about it:

Which action writes that timestamp?

If the answer is "somebody read the record", you do not have a freshness
signal. You have a popularity signal wearing a freshness label, and the things
you look at most will always look like the things that are most true.

That was us, for months, in a product whose entire job is to remember things
accurately.

What we found

We build a memory layer for coding agents. Every stored lesson carries a
confidence badge, and the badge decays with age: green for about a day and a
half, amber after that, red from day ten. The agent sees it on every recall. It is supposed to
say how much should you trust this.

We went looking for why nobody acted on the amber ones. The badge hangs off a
field called verified_at, so we read the code that writes it. Here is what
recall_best_solution did, on every single call:

const updatedLesson = {
  ...lesson,
  recall_count: (lesson.recall_count ?? 0) + 1,
  verified_at: recalledAt,      // ← every read
  last_recalled_at: recalledAt,
  confidence: 1.0,              // ← every read
};

Reading a lesson reset its confidence clock to 1.0 and stamped it as verified.
The comment above it even said so, cheerfully: "Recall resets verified_at
(confidence clock restart)." Somebody wrote that on purpose, and the reasoning
is not stupid — if an agent recalled it and did not complain, maybe it is still
good. But "nobody complained" is not verification, and the field is not called
nobody_complained_at.

Then we counted, on a real store of 735 entries:

471  (64.1 %)  carried a verified_at LATER than the day they were written
120            would have been stale by age and were showing as fresh
 21 days       median age by write date
 14 days       median age by "verified"

Reading had shaved a week off the apparent age of the entire store. And the
distribution is the worst possible one: the entries that get read most are the
ones that look freshest, so the badge was brightest exactly where a wrong
answer would do the most damage.

The class of bug, not the instance

Ours is a memory product, so this reads like our specific mistake. It is not.
Look for this shape anywhere:

  • A monitoring dashboard whose "last check" updates when you open the page.
  • A dependency audit whose "reviewed" date is set by the CI job that lists dependencies, not by anyone reviewing them.
  • A runbook with "verified working" in the frontmatter and a date that moves every time someone copies a command out of it.
  • A cache entry whose TTL refreshes on read, in a place where you meant it to expire on age.

The common shape: a field whose name asserts something, written by an action
that does not do that thing. It is close kin to the guard that has never
fired and the alert nobody has read, with one extra twist — this one does not
stay silent. It actively reports good news.

That is why it survives so long. A broken check that goes quiet gets noticed
eventually, when someone asks why it never says anything. A broken check that
says "fine" gets thanked.

The check, and it takes two minutes

Pick your freshness field. Then:

  1. Find every write to it. grep -rn "verified_at" src/ and read each one. Not the reads. The writes.
  2. For each write, ask what the caller was doing. If any of them is a read path, a page render, a list endpoint, a health poll — that is your bug.
  3. Then check the distribution. Compare the field against the record's own creation date. If a large share sits later, something other than verification is moving it.

The third step is the one that gave us our number, and it needs one query. Ours
was: how many entries carry a verified_at after their ts? The answer was 64
per cent, and it took about a minute to get.

If yours comes back near zero, you are fine and you have spent two minutes. If
it comes back high, you have just learned that the age everyone quotes in
planning meetings is fiction.

What we changed, and what it cost

Both fields already existed, separately. The fix was to stop writing one of
them:

const updatedLesson = {
  ...lesson,
  recall_count: (lesson.recall_count ?? 0) + 1,
  last_recalled_at: recalledAt,   // reading counts itself, and nothing else
};

verified_at now means what it says: the moment the entry was written or
actually re-checked. Age calculation falls back to the write date when the
field is absent, which is the honest default.

The cost is visible and we took it on purpose: about 120 entries went from
amber to red overnight. Nothing about them changed. They had been old the
whole time, and the badge had been lying about it.

That is the part worth sitting with, because it is the reason this kind of bug
gets built in the first place. The honest version of the signal looks worse.
Somebody, at some point, will look at a dashboard that went red and ask what
broke — and the answer is "nothing broke, we stopped pretending".

The second half, which we nearly missed

A wall of red warnings with no way forward gets clicked past just as reliably
as a badge that always says green. We had swapped one useless state for
another.

The fix came from a stranger in a comment thread, who had started storing, next
to each of his own notes, the command that re-checks it — and found two already
wrong on the first day. So our badge now carries the entry's first stored
command:

before  🔴 STALE (21d old, confidence 50% — likely outdated!)
after   🔴 STALE (21d old, confidence 50% — likely outdated!,
                  e.g. `curl -s http://localhost:8080/health`)

No new field: the command was already stored on most entries, because
operational lessons come with the call that proves them. A field we would have
had to ask people to fill would have gone the way of every other optional
field — we have one in the same store that is populated on 2 records out of
735.

One line we will not cross: the server never runs that command. A stored
command that a service executes on its own is a back door in anything shared.
It gets shown. The human or the agent runs it.

The one sentence

A field that reports trust has to be written by something that earns it.

If you only take one thing from this: go and find out which action writes your
verified_at. It is a grep and a query. We did not do it for months, and for
months our own product quietly told us that everything we had looked at
recently was true.

Next in this series: I sent five AI agents to read my repo, and every one of them ran on my most expensive model.

Which field in your system says "verified", and what actually writes it?

I build cachly. It keeps what you explain to your AI: your rules, your decisions and the bugs you already solved. Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot and the others read it in every session, for you alone or for your whole team, and every lesson carries the name of whoever learned it.

Try it, in increasing order of commitment:

  • 30 seconds, no account: npx @cachly-dev/mcp-server@latest demo in any git repo. It reads your log locally and prints what an assistant would already know about the project. After npx fetches the package, the command makes no network calls.
  • Claude Code plugin: /plugin marketplace add cachly-dev/cachly-mcp, then /plugin install cachly-brain@cachly.
  • 5 minutes, free tier: npx @cachly-dev/mcp-server@latest autopilot writes the MCP configuration for whichever assistant you use.
  • Or from the web: cachly.dev · free tier, servers in Germany.

On Product Hunt from 1 December: cachly on Product Hunt. Follow it there if you want a note on launch day.

articles.title: My AI swore all tests passed. Here's the free one-file fix that makes it prove it.
articles.description: My agent told me "All tests pass." It had run 74 of our 105 test files. Another time it wrote "The...
articles.body_html:
My agent told me "All tests pass." It had run 74 of our 105 test files. Another time it wrote "The email went out at 08:45." The clock said 08:37. A third time: "14 people clicked Sign in." Those were page views. Nobody had counted clicks.

None of that was lying. The agent said what it believed. The trouble is that "done" is a sentence, and a sentence costs nothing to write.

So I stopped accepting sentences. A task is done when one command exits 0. The command writes a receipt, and the agent pastes the receipt instead of the word "done". Here is the free version of that, in a single file.

What you get

proof-gate is one Node file. No dependencies, MIT, 8 tests of its own. It does two things for every task:

  1. It runs your checks (tests, build, lint, anything with an exit code).
  2. It writes a receipt: the commit, the time, every command and its exit code.

It works the same with Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot or a plain shell. It does not talk to any model. It only reads exit codes.

Step 1: put the file in your repo 

git clone https://github.com/cachly-dev/proof-gate
cp proof-gate/proof-gate.mjs ./proof-gate.mjs

You need Node 18 or newer. That is the whole install.

Step 2: describe one task

Create proof-gate.json in your project root. This one guards a rate limiter:

{
  "tasks": {
    "rate-limit": {
      "checks": [
        { "name": "acceptance", "run": "node --test test/rate-limit.test.mjs" },
        { "name": "build", "run": "npm run build" }
      ],
      "controls": [
        {
          "name": "says no when the limit is off",
          "run": "node --test test/rate-limit.test.mjs",
          "env": { "RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED": "1" }
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}

The controls block is the part people skip, so one line on it. A control is the same check pointed at something that is supposed to be wrong. It must fail. If it passes, the gate goes red, because a check that cannot fail proves nothing. I cover that in a separate post. For now, copy the block and adapt it.

Step 3: run it 

node proof-gate.mjs rate-limit

TASK: rate-limit
GATE: 0 (3/3)
RECEIPT: .proof-gate/receipts/rate-limit.json
NOTE: -

Four lines. Exit code 0 means green, 1 means red, 2 means refused (the setup is incomplete and nothing was judged). Refused is never green.

When something is wrong you get the first problem in NOTE:

TASK: rate-limit
GATE: 1 (2/3)
RECEIPT: .proof-gate/receipts/rate-limit.json
NOTE: control passed, so the check cannot say no: says no when the limit is off

Step 4: make the agent hand over the receipt

Add this to CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md or your Cursor rules:

## Done means
- A task is done when `node proof-gate.mjs <task>` exits 0. Paste its four lines.
- If the gate is red, say so. Do not call the task done.

That is the change. The agent can still be wrong, but it can no longer be wrong quietly.

Why a receipt and not just the exit code

The receipt is .proof-gate/receipts/rate-limit.json. It holds the commit hash, a dirty flag, the time, and the last 20 lines of output from every command.

On 24 November my own worker agent reported "gate green". I looked at the receipt. The commit in it was the one before the agent's change. The agent had run the gate before it committed, so the green belonged to the old code. Without the commit in the receipt I would have believed it.

The same day, a feature gate of mine was green with 6 of 6 steps. The full server tests were red. One of them requires that every server route has a caller in the app, or a written reason why not. My gate had never included the full tests. I found it before the push, and now the full test run is part of the gate. A gate is only as honest as the list of things in it, and the receipt makes that list visible. If the checks you expected are not in the receipt, you see it.

Where it runs

The gate is a plain command, so it fits wherever you can run a shell command:

  • In Claude Code, the agent runs it itself. The rule in CLAUDE.md tells it to.
  • In Cursor or Copilot, put the same rule in your rules file or instructions, and run the gate yourself if the agent does not.
  • In CI, add one line: node proof-gate.mjs rate-limit. The exit code decides whether the job passes.

You can also run it after the agent says "done" and before you read a single line of the diff. If it is red, you saved yourself the reading.

What it is not

  • Not a test runner. It calls yours.
  • Not an AI judge. Every decision comes from an exit code.
  • Receipts keep the last 20 lines of each command's output. Keep secrets out of your test output, or add .proof-gate/receipts/ to .gitignore.

Try it tonight

Pick one task you gave an agent this week. Write its proof-gate.json entry with one check and one control. Run it. Two things can happen. It goes green and you now have a receipt. Or it goes red or refused, and you just learned something about a task you thought was finished.

The repo is here: github.com/cachly-dev/proof-gate. There is also a full version, free: the Agent Proof Kit, with task packs, a model ladder and a ledger around the gate. Leave your address at cachly.dev/forge and the download link arrives after you confirm. That is all I will say about it here.

What is the last "done" from an agent that turned out not to be?

I build cachly. It keeps what you explain to your AI: your rules, your decisions and the bugs you already solved. Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot and the others read it in every session, for you alone or for your whole team, and every lesson carries the name of whoever learned it.

Try it, in increasing order of commitment:

  • 30 seconds, no account: npx @cachly-dev/mcp-server@latest demo in any git repo. It reads your log locally and prints what an assistant would already know about the project. After npx fetches the package, the command makes no network calls.
  • Claude Code plugin: /plugin marketplace add cachly-dev/cachly-mcp, then /plugin install cachly-brain@cachly.
  • 5 minutes, free tier: npx @cachly-dev/mcp-server@latest autopilot writes the MCP configuration for whichever assistant you use.
  • Or from the web: cachly.dev · free tier, servers in Germany.

On Product Hunt from 1 December: cachly on Product Hunt. Follow it there if you want a note on launch day.

articles.title: Ask in Russian, and Coding Agents Upgrade Your Library Less Than Half as Often
articles.description: Your migration guide is on the web. An agent upgrading your library reads it only if it decides to...
articles.body_html:
Your migration guide is on the web. An agent upgrading your library reads it only if it decides to search, and many runs never do. In my last round, whether an agent searched depended on the agent, on the model, and on something maintainers rarely think about: the language the user wrote the task in.

This is a follow-up to Coding agents keep installing the old version of your library. That piece was about where agents pick a version. This one asks what changes when the user doesn't write in English, and what a maintainer can do about it.

The test

Two upgrade tasks, each a small working project on the old version:

  • Hedera. "Update the Hedera SDK to the current supported version." The supported SDK moved from @hashgraph/sdk to @hiero-ledger/sdk, and the old name still shows as latest on npm, not deprecated. To pass, the agent has to find the new name.
  • Prisma. "Upgrade Prisma to version 8." Prisma 8 has no @prisma/client: the client is now @prisma/orm-postgres, while @prisma/client@latest still points to 7.

Four agents: Codex (GPT-6-Sol, effort low), Claude Code with Haiku 5.5, Kimi Code with K3.1, and Claude Code with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. The same task text in English, Spanish, Ukrainian and Russian, with code and package names left in English. Three setups: no help, four lines in AGENTS.md, or a colleague's note about a similar case. Five runs per cell, a hidden grader for each run, 591 graded runs in total.

Searching decided the result

Without help, on Hedera, 13 of the 15 runs that searched the web found the new package. Of the 65 that didn't search, 7 did. npm view @hashgraph/sdk version says nothing about the move; the announcement does, and it's on the web.

The language changed whether the agent searched

Share of runs without help that actually upgraded the library:

Across both tasks: English 21 of 39, Spanish 19 of 39, Ukrainian 17 of 40, Russian 8 of 39. The gap between English and Russian is unlikely to be chance (Fisher's exact test, p = 0.005). Spanish and Ukrainian sit between the two.

Codex shows it most clearly. Runs without help in which it searched at least once, both tasks together:

With the task in English, Codex searched and passed Hedera 5 times out of 5. With the same task in Russian, it never searched and passed 0 of 5. I found the same pattern a few weeks earlier on different tasks, and I still don't know why it is Russian in particular: Ukrainian uses the same alphabet, and Codex searched there. If you have a theory, I'd like to hear it.

The model matters too. Inside the same Claude Code, without help, Haiku passed 3 of 20 runs on Prisma and DeepSeek 18 of 20. Haiku searched in 2 runs of 40, DeepSeek in 10.

Four lines in AGENTS.md closed the gap

These four lines, in English, in every language arm:

When you add or update a dependency:

1. Before you pick a package or a version, run the full `npm view <package>`
   and read `deprecated` and the dist-tags, not only `version`.
2. Check whether the package has moved to a new name.
3. Read the docs that ship inside the package (AGENTS.md, README, type files)
   before the website.
4. Search the web for the official upgrade guide before you change code.

With them, every agent passed every run in every language: Hedera 80 of 80, Prisma 76 of 76. Codex with the Russian task searched in 9 runs of 10, up from 0. Haiku searched in 36 of 40, up from 2. The colleague's note passed everything too.

These lines live in your users' projects, not in your package, and most users won't have them.

The same lines can read your tags differently than you meant

The first version of the Prisma task said "upgrade to the current version", not "version 8". There, the four lines barely helped: 13 of 80 runs. The agents did exactly what the lines asked. They read the dist-tags, saw that prisma@latest is 8.0.0-rc.33, a release candidate, while @prisma/client@latest is still 7.10.1, and most of them wrote in their answer that they were staying on the stable 7.10.1 on purpose. That's a reasonable call. Only the note, which says plainly that current Prisma is 8, got them there.

An agent that reads your dist-tags carefully takes them at their word. If latest points at a release candidate next to a stable 7 on another package, careful agents will choose 7.

What a maintainer can do

A user's agent that skips the search still reads npm, the install output and the package itself. Put the upgrade facts there and they reach users in every language:

  1. Deprecate the old package with a message that names the new one. npm deprecate shows up in the install output and in the full npm view. In Hedera's case npm says nothing, so only a search finds the move.
  2. Ship one last release of the old package whose README says where it moved. The README is what an agent reads after installing it.
  3. Decide what latest means, and keep related packages consistent. A release candidate on latest with the client still on 7 sends careful agents back to 7.
  4. Ship the upgrade note inside the package. Docs in the package were read; docs sites mostly weren't.
  5. Publish a few lines your users can copy into AGENTS.md. The four above, or your own version naming your package. They worked in every language I tried.

The previous article has the measurements behind items 1 to 4.

If you want to see what agents do with your own package, including with tasks in other languages, Ready for Agents runs these checks for library teams.

Limits

Two tasks, both on npm. Five runs per cell, so a single cell says little; the language gap holds across both tasks together, and the four-line result holds in all 32 cells. The Spanish and Ukrainian prompts were machine-translated and checked by two models, not by native speakers. Kimi is missing 9 runs on the Prisma task because of subscription limits. Effort is the default for every agent except Codex (low).

Scripts and the table of every cell: worklore-mcp.

articles.title: Saving Every Sixty Seconds Is Not Saving Your Work
articles.description: At 00:09:44 the timer saved. At 00:09:50 the third fix finished. Six seconds.  That is the whole...
articles.body_html:
At 00:09:44 the timer saved. At 00:09:50 the third fix finished. Six seconds.

That is the whole story, and everything below is me measuring what those six seconds cost. The timer saved a patch that did not have the third fix in it. The kill came at 00:10:19, before the next tick, and the window that held the finished, tested fix is gone. The fix was done. It was green. It is not in the patch, and there is no way to get it back except doing it again.

itsvicmoreno asked the question that made me run this. Under the last piece, the one about saving the patch after every step, he asked what happens if you save on a timer instead. A patch every sixty seconds, not after each step. On a longer job, how much does the timer version leave behind when the work dies between saves? I told him I would try it. Then he came back with a second point, and it is the sharper one: on a repo-wide rename, save before the test run, not after, because a test run that hangs takes the patch with it. So this run tests both. Same job, two ways of saving, a rename in the middle, and I killed the work myself both times so the kill point was not chosen to flatter either side.

The job was a small cart helper, ten steps. Nine one-line fixes, the kind where you read the failing test, change one line, and watch it go green, plus one rename in the middle where a function changes its name across two files. Twelve tests, two passing at the start, ten failing. Each step took about twenty seconds of reading and checking, so the whole job runs a few minutes, which is the point. The last piece proved the shape on a two-line fix. A two-line fix does not have enough room between saves for a timer to miss anything. Ten steps does.

The first version saved the patch after every step, the same shape as the last piece. Fix the line, save the patch, run the tests, write the result down, move on. I killed it at 144 seconds, in the middle of step six, before that step's edit had even started. Five steps were done and all five were in the patch. Getting back to green from a fresh copy took 2.17 seconds: take the template, apply the patch, run the tests. Eight of twelve tests passing, and the recovered file was identical to the one in the dead window, byte for byte. Nothing about the recovery depended on the window still being alive, because nothing about the saving did either.

The second version saved on a sixty-second timer and nothing else. Same ten steps, same pace. A background save every sixty seconds, no save after a step, no matter how finished the step was. I killed it at 95 seconds, in the middle of step five. Four steps were done. Four steps had been tested and were green. The patch had two of them.

Here is what that looks like, as numbered problems, because each one is a different way the timer fails.

  1. The timer loses finished work, and finished is the wrong word for what it loses. Steps three and four were not half done. Step three changed a line that added price and quantity instead of multiplying them. Step four changed a discount that subtracted the percent number instead of taking a percentage off. Both were edited, both were tested, both were green, both are in the test log I kept. The patch has neither. The work the timer lost is not the work in progress. It is the work you already finished and already proved, which is worse, because that is the work you stop thinking about. Step three missed the save by 5.9 seconds. Not a minute. Six seconds.

  2. The two records disagreed, and the wrong one looked healthier. The test log said seven of twelve passing. The patch said five. If you only read the log, you would think you had four steps banked. You had two. A log is a diary. A patch is the work. On the per-edit version the two always agreed, because the save and the test happened in the same step. On the timer version they drift apart by up to sixty seconds, and the drift is silent. Nothing warns you. The next tick would have fixed it, and the next tick never came.

  3. The timer's gap is bounded, and the bound is the wrong comfort. Sixty seconds is the most it can lose, and that sounds small until you ask what you can finish in sixty seconds. Two steps, in this run, forty-two seconds of green-tested work. On a real job, an hour of steps fits between the same two ticks if the kill lands late in the interval, and the interval does not care how much you did. It only cares when the clock says save. The bound is real. It bounds the wrong thing. It bounds time, and what you lose is work.

  4. The rename is where itsvicmoreno's second point lands, and it landed harder than I expected. The two random kills both fell before step seven, so the rename never ran in either main arm. I ran the timer version a third time and killed it right after the rename finished, to get the measurement. The rename took 26.31 seconds, the longest step in that run, and the patch was saved before the test run started. I can show the order in the timestamps: the patch file was written at 00:14:02, the test result was logged after it. If that test run had hung, the rename would already have been on disk. That is the whole rule. A rename touches two files and the test run after it is the one that can sit there forever, so the save goes before the test, not after it. In the timer version, that save is the only save that is not on the clock, and it is the only reason the rename survived. The timer would have caught it at the next tick, maybe. Maybe is doing a lot of work in that sentence.

The comparison, in one table:

Save after each step Save every 60 seconds
Kill point 144 s, mid-step 6 95 s, mid-step 5
Steps finished before the kill 5 4
Steps in the patch 5 2
Steps lost 0 2 (steps 3 and 4)
Recovery time 2.17 s 3.11 s
Tests passing after recovery 8 of 12 5 of 12

The recovery times are nearly the same, and that is worth saying plainly, because it is not where the difference lives. Applying a patch is cheap either way. The difference is what is in the patch when you apply it. The per-edit version recovered everything it had finished. The timer version recovered half of what it had finished, and the half it lost was the half it had finished most recently, which is the half you remember worst when you sit down to redo it.

The redo is the part nobody prices. Steps three and four are each one line. Typing them again takes seconds, and that is the number people quote when they say the timer is fine. But the redo is not the typing. It is remembering which two lines, out of ten, were the ones that did not make it. The test log says four steps were done and green. The patch says two. You have to work out which two are missing, and the only way to do that is to read the log against the patch line by line, then run the tests again to prove the retyped lines are the same ones. On this toy the whole thing takes a minute. On a real job the missing steps are not two lines with labels on them. They are the hours you spent finding the right line, and the only record of which line it was is a log entry that says it passed. The timer does not just lose the edit. It loses the proof that the edit was the right one, and the proof is the expensive part.

One more number, because itsvicmoreno asked for it and the last piece could not give it to him. The longest single step across all three runs was 46.23 seconds, step two of the per-edit version. It was not the edit. The edit was one line, the same as every other step. It was the test run going slow that once, about twenty-seven seconds against two to four for every other step's test run, for no reason I could find. That is the honest answer to his question, and it is also the reason the timer loses: the step that eats the interval is never the step you planned for. The rename, the step he was asking about, took 26.31 seconds. The slow test took 46. So if you are counting on a sixty-second gap being small, remember that one slow test run is most of it.

There are limits here and I would rather name them than let a reader find them. One random kill per version is two draws, not a distribution. The gap of two lost steps is what this draw produced. What carries over is the shape, not the count: a timer loses everything since the last tick, and the last tick is never when you need it. The pacing of the steps was set by me, eighteen seconds of reading and checking per step, so the job would run a few minutes. The edits and the tests are real, the thinking time is staged, and I am saying that plainly. The kill was staged by me in all three runs, and the reason a real stall happens stays unknown in a way my staged kill does not capture. And the recovery times are seconds because the test suite is twelve tests. On a real repo the seconds grow. The steps do not come back with them.

So here is the claim, and it is the one you can argue with: saving every sixty seconds is not saving your work. It is betting that nothing kills the work in the sixty seconds after you finish a step, and the bet gets worse the more steps you finish, because each finished step is another thing the next tick has not seen yet. Save after the step. Save the rename before the test. The timer can stay, as a backstop, but a backstop is not a plan.

What do you save, and when? If you have a timer running, has it ever actually saved you, or has it only ever saved most of you? And what is the longest single step you have watched eat a whole interval, a test run that would not finish, a rename across more files than you expected? I want the numbers, not the theory. The theory I already had. The theory said sixty seconds was fine.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: Putting the Last-Read Time on the Diff Doesn't Catch a Stale Read
articles.description: A timestamp on the approval diff does not catch a stale read. I know, because I put one there and...
articles.body_html:
A timestamp on the approval diff does not catch a stale read. I know, because I put one there and watched the reviewer walk straight past it twelve times. Then I added the flag itsvicmoreno asked for, the line that says the read is past the limit, and the reviewer still held everything. The flag changed something real. It just was not the verdict.

The setup is the same order from the last piece about approvals. Order ORD-2091, a refund of $12, amount $49 down to $37, one Python book at $29 and one video pack at $20. The reviewer sees only the diff: the proposed change, then the agreed fields as read from the provider record, then when the record was last read. What the reviewer never sees is what changed after that read. In ten of the twelve trials the provider record had moved. The amount was now $41, an $8 adjustment already landed. Or the status was now refunded, the refund already went through. Or the video pack was gone from the order. The read was between 25 minutes and 8 hours old. Two trials were fresh controls, nothing had changed since the read, 12 and 35 minutes old. A hold on a stale trial is a catch. A hold on a fresh control is a false alarm. An approval on a stale trial is the miss the whole test is about.

The reviewer is a small local model, Qwen 2.5 with 1.5 billion parameters, answering at temperature zero, one word first, APPROVE or HOLD, then one sentence saying why. Small on purpose. A big model would have opinions about everything and I would not know which part of the diff moved it. A small one has fewer places to hide.

Arm A carried a plain timestamp and nothing else. "Provider record last read: 2026-11-24 12:35 (25 min ago)." Eight of the ten stale trials came back held, and the other two never came back at all, the calls timed out after five minutes each. I am counting those as errors, not catches, because no verdict arrived. The two fresh controls both came back held. So in arm A the reviewer held ten out of ten completed trials, stale and fresh alike, and never once mentioned the age of the read in any reply. Not once in ten. The reasons it gave were about the refund itself. The amount dropping from $49 to $37 is a significant reduction. The status is paid, so it cannot be refunded. The book alone is not a complete purchase. Every one of those reasons is wrong about this order, the customer agreed to exactly this change, but they are the reasons a cautious reviewer reaches for when the diff gives it nothing better to hold onto. The timestamp was on the page the whole time. The reviewer read past it like it was a footer.

Arm B added the flag itsvicmoreno suggested in his follow-up: past the sixty-minute limit, the diff gains a line in plain language. "STALE READ, provider record read 1 hour 35 minutes ago, past the 60-minute limit. Read it again before approving." Nine of the ten stale trials came back held, one timed out, and both fresh controls timed out too, so arm B has no control data at all and I am saying that plainly instead of borrowing arm A's. But the nine replies that did come back split in a way the verdicts never show. Below the limit, at 25 and 40 minutes, the reviewer gave the same refund reasoning as arm A. Past the limit, at 95 minutes and beyond, every single reply cited the age and the limit. "The provider record was read 1 hour and 35 minutes ago, which is past the 60-minute limit." "The provider record was read 8 hours ago, which is past the 60-minute limit." Word for word, the flag became the reason.

Here is the table, because the verdicts alone would mislead you.

Plain timestamp Timestamp plus flag
Stale trials held 8 of 8 completed 9 of 9 completed
Stale trials missed (approved) 0 0
Fresh controls held 2 of 2 no data, both timed out
Fresh controls approved 0 no data
Calls that timed out 2 of 12 3 of 12
Replies mentioning the read age 0 of 10 6 of 9

Read that table the wrong way and you conclude the flag changed nothing. Nine holds either way, zero misses either way. Read it the right way and the flag is the only thing in the whole run that changed anything at all. Without it, the reviewer held a stale read for the wrong reason, the size of the refund. With it, the reviewer held a stale read for the right reason, the read is old. The verdict is identical. The explanation is not, and the explanation is what the next person in the queue acts on. A hold that says "the refund looks big" sends someone to re-check the refund. A hold that says "the read is eight hours old" sends someone to re-read the provider record. Only one of those fixes the actual problem.

But the controls are the part that keeps me from recommending the flag and walking away. Both fresh controls in arm A came back held, on reads 12 and 35 minutes old, with nothing changed. The reviewer held a change it should have approved, for the same refund reasoning it used on the stale trials. So a HOLD from this reviewer tells you nothing about whether the read was stale. It tells you the reviewer holds things. If your approval queue runs on a reviewer like this, the timestamp and the flag do not make the queue faster or more accurate. They make the holds explain themselves. That is worth having, and it is not the thing itsvicmoreno asked for. He asked whether the timestamp catches a stale read. On this evidence, it does not catch anything, because there was nothing to catch. The reviewer was already holding.

There are limits here and they are not small. One reviewer, one order, one change shape, twelve trials per arm, five calls lost to timeouts. The timeouts clustered near the end of the run, which smells like the machine getting tired rather than the trials getting harder, and I am not going to pretend I know which. A human reviewer might read the timestamp where this one did not. A bigger model might too, or it might hold everything for better reasons. The sixty-minute limit was my choice, not a measured one. What I can stand behind is narrower: on this reviewer, the plain timestamp never entered the reasoning, the flag always did once it appeared, and neither changed a single verdict, because the verdicts were already all holds.

So here is the claim, and it is the one you can argue with: put the last-read time on the diff, and put the flag on it past the limit, but do not tell yourself you have fixed stale approvals. You have fixed the explanation for the hold. The stale approval you are worried about is the one the reviewer approves, and this reviewer never approved anything, fresh or stale. If your reviewer approves fresh changes and holds stale ones, the flag might be the thing that tips it. Mine did not, and the honest read is that the flag is worth adding for the reason it gives, not the verdict it changes.

itsvicmoreno's follow-up asked which source the test approves against, and that is the provider object the diff is built on, the same record the timestamp describes. He also asked where the line goes for a balance, and I do not have an answer yet. The line goes under the fields it describes, is the best I can say.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: CORS with Cookies Between Next.js and a NestJS API: Preflights, Credentials, and When to Proxy Instead — Field Notes
articles.description: Headline: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser rule that decides whether page...
articles.body_html:
Headline: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser rule that decides whether page JavaScript may read a response from another origin; it does not stop the request from reaching your server. For a Next.js frontend calling a NestJS API with cookies, either return the exact origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true and a 2xx preflight, or proxy /api through a Next.js rewrite so the browser never makes a cross-origin call.

Every project where I split a Next.js frontend from a NestJS API hits the same three CORS errors, in order: the preflight fails, the wildcard origin is rejected once cookies are involved, and then every call returns 200 while the user stays logged out because the session cookie never travels. Here is what each failure means and the setup I ended up with.

Key takeaways

  • CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server: it controls whether page JavaScript can read a cross-origin response, and it does not stop the request from reaching your API.
  • A JSON Content-Type, an Authorization header, or a PUT/PATCH/DELETE method makes a request non-simple, so the browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight — without cookies — and needs a 2xx response with matching allow headers.
  • Credentialed requests (credentials: 'include') require Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true plus the exact requesting origin; Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * is rejected.
  • Cookies cross origins only when the request opts in and SameSite allows it; across different sites that means SameSite=None; Secure, which Safari's default third-party cookie blocking still defeats.
  • Proxying /api/* through a Next.js rewrite makes the API same-origin: no preflights and first-party cookies, at the cost of one extra network hop.

What does CORS actually protect?

CORS protects the user's data inside the browser, not your server. An origin is the combination of scheme, host, and port, so https://app.example.com and https://api.example.com are different origins. The same-origin policy stops a page on one origin from reading responses from another, and CORS response headers are how a server opts specific origins back in.

Three consequences took me too long to internalize:

  • Only browsers enforce CORS. curl, Postman, a Next.js Server Component, and a NestJS service calling another service never send preflights or check Access-Control-* headers.
  • A blocked request may still have run. For a simple cross-origin request, the browser sends it, the server executes it, and only the response is hidden from JavaScript.
  • CORS is not CSRF protection. A forged form POST from another site still reaches the API with whatever cookies the browser attaches; SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens, or an Origin header check are what stop it.

Same-origin and same-site are different tests, and cookies follow the same-site test. A site is the scheme plus the registrable domain (eTLD+1, such as example.com), and ports do not count:

Request from Request to Same-origin? Same-site?
https://app.example.com https://api.example.com No — host differs Yes — both on example.com
http://localhost:3000 http://localhost:4000 No — port differs Yes — ports do not count
https://shop.vercel.app https://shop-api.vercel.app No No — vercel.app is a public suffix

Why does my fetch trigger a preflight OPTIONS request?

The browser sends an OPTIONS preflight before any cross-origin request that is not "simple". A simple request uses GET, HEAD, or POST, sets only CORS-safelisted headers, and sends a Content-Type of text/plain, multipart/form-data, or application/x-www-form-urlencoded. A JSON body, an Authorization header, a custom header such as Idempotency-Key, or a PUT, PATCH, or DELETE method each force a preflight, so almost every real API call gets one:

await fetch('https://api.example.com/api/orders', {
  method: 'POST',
  credentials: 'include', // send and store cookies cross-origin
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, // not simple → preflight
  body: JSON.stringify(order),
});

The preflight announces the method and headers in Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers. The server must answer with a 2xx status plus Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods, and Access-Control-Allow-Headers values that cover them. Preflight requests never carry cookies or an Authorization header. My first failure came from exactly that rule: an auth middleware registered with app.use() above app.enableCors() answered every preflight with 401, and the browser reported it as a CORS error.

Access-Control-Max-Age sets how long the browser caches a preflight result. Without the header, the Fetch spec default is 5 seconds; Chromium caps the value at 7200 seconds and Firefox at 86400 seconds.

Why can't I use Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with cookies?

A credentialed request — fetch(url, { credentials: 'include' }) or XMLHttpRequest.withCredentials = true — is readable only when the response sends Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true and an Access-Control-Allow-Origin equal to the requesting origin. Chrome rejects the wildcard with: "The value of the 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header in the response must not be the wildcard '' when the request's credentials mode is 'include'." For credentialed requests, a ` in Access-Control-Allow-Headers, Access-Control-Allow-Methods, or Access-Control-Expose-Headers` is treated as a literal name, not a wildcard.

The tempting fix is to reflect whatever Origin arrives — origin: true in the cors package that NestJS uses with the Express adapter. Combined with credentials: true, reflection lets any website read authenticated responses for a logged-in user. I use an exact allowlist from an environment variable instead:

// main.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

const allowedOrigins = new Set(
  (process.env.CORS_ORIGIN ?? '').split(',').map((o) => o.trim()).filter(Boolean),
);

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
  app.enableCors({
    origin: (origin, callback) => {
      // No Origin header: curl, server-to-server calls — CORS does not apply
      if (!origin || allowedOrigins.has(origin)) return callback(null, true);
      callback(null, false); // omit CORS headers; the browser blocks the read
    },
    credentials: true, // Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
    methods: ['GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'PATCH', 'DELETE'],
    allowedHeaders: ['Content-Type', 'Authorization', 'Idempotency-Key'],
    exposedHeaders: ['ETag', 'X-Request-Id'],
    maxAge: 7200, // Chromium's cap for preflight caching
  });
  await app.listen(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
}
void bootstrap();

The details in that config that matter:

  • callback(null, false), not an Error. Returning false omits the CORS headers and lets the browser block the read; passing an Error turns the request into a 500 under Express.
  • Exact strings only. A suffix regex like /example\.com$/ also matches https://evil-example.com, and allowlisting null admits every sandboxed iframe and file:// page, because those send Origin: null.
  • Vary: Origin on every reflected response. The cors package adds it automatically; a hand-written middleware must add it too, or a CDN can serve one origin's Access-Control-Allow-Origin to another.
  • Response headers are opt-in. JavaScript can read only CORS-safelisted response headers such as Content-Type; ETag and X-Request-Id stay invisible until listed in Access-Control-Expose-Headers.

Why are my cookies not sent on cross-origin requests?

A cookie crosses origins only when three layers agree: the request opts in, the cookie's SameSite attribute allows the context, and the browser's third-party cookie policy allows it. fetch() defaults to credentials: 'same-origin', so a cross-origin call needs credentials: 'include' before the browser sends any cookie or stores any Set-Cookie from the response.

When the frontend and API share a site — app.example.com and api.example.com — the request is same-site, and SameSite=Lax cookies are sent. Chrome treats a cookie with no SameSite attribute as Lax. A cookie set by api.example.com without a Domain attribute is host-only, so Next.js middleware on app.example.com cannot read it; Domain=example.com shares it with both hosts.

When they are different sites — such as two *.vercel.app deployments, because vercel.app is on the Public Suffix List — the session cookie becomes a third-party cookie. It needs SameSite=None; Secure, and even then Safari blocks third-party cookies by default and Chrome blocks them in Incognito. I stopped shipping cross-site cookie auth: either the API moves to a subdomain of the frontend's site, or the frontend proxies it.

When should I proxy API calls through a Next.js rewrite instead of enabling CORS?

Proxy through a Next.js rewrite when one frontend owns the API; keep CORS when several origins, a mobile app, or third parties call the API directly. A rewrite lets the browser call /api/... on its own origin while the Next.js server forwards the request to the backend, so there is no preflight, no CORS header, and every cookie is first-party:

// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from 'next';

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  async rewrites() {
    return [
      {
        source: '/api/:path*',
        destination: `${process.env.API_URL}/api/:path*`,
      },
    ];
  },
};

export default nextConfig;

The browser now calls fetch('/api/me') with the default credentials: 'same-origin'. A rewrites array runs after Next.js checks its own routes, so a local app/api route handler with the same path still wins. Two backend changes came with the switch: session cookies must be host-only, because the browser rejects Domain=api.example.com on the frontend's host; and rate limiting or logging must read the client IP from X-Forwarded-For instead of the socket address.

Direct CORS Next.js rewrite proxy
Preflight On every non-simple request, cached up to Access-Control-Max-Age None — requests are same-origin
Cookies Need credentials: 'include'; cross-site needs SameSite=None; Secure and fails under third-party cookie blocking First-party; SameSite=Lax works
Network path Browser → API Browser → Next.js → API (one extra hop)
Configuration Origin allowlist on the API for every environment One API_URL variable on the frontend

Why does a 500 error show up as a CORS error?

A failed response without Access-Control-Allow-Origin is reported as a CORS error, which hides the real status code. JavaScript receives only a generic TypeError — "Failed to fetch" in Chrome — with no status. The usual causes are an error handler or gateway that responds before the CORS middleware runs, and nginx: add_header applies only to 2xx and 3xx responses unless the directive ends with always.

When a CORS error appears, I check the Network tab for the real status first, then replay the preflight with curl:

# Replay the preflight a browser would send
curl -i -X OPTIONS https://api.example.com/api/orders \
  -H 'Origin: https://app.example.com' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: POST' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type'

A correct response returns 204 with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com, Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, and an Access-Control-Allow-Headers value that includes content-type. If those headers are missing, the fix belongs on the server or the proxy, not in the frontend fetch() call.

FAQ

Q: Why does my API work in Postman or curl but fail in the browser?

A: CORS is enforced only by browsers. curl and Postman never send preflights or check Access-Control-* headers, so a missing or wrong CORS configuration shows up only when page JavaScript calls the API.

Q: Does mode: 'no-cors' fix a CORS error?

A: No. mode: 'no-cors' returns an opaque response with status 0 and an unreadable body, and it allows only simple requests. It silences the error by hiding the data.

Q: Is CORS a CSRF protection?

A: No. Simple cross-origin requests, such as an HTML form POST, still reach the server with cookies attached; CORS only stops the attacker's page from reading the response. Use SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens, or an Origin header check against CSRF.
