articles.title: How Unicode Font Generators Work Under the Hood in Fontaly
articles.description: If you have ever seen bold, italic, or cursive text inside an Instagram bio or a Discord username,...
articles.body_html:
If you have ever seen bold, italic, or cursive text inside an Instagram bio or a Discord username, you might wonder how that works in plain-text fields that do not support HTML or CSS. Those styles are not actual font files at all. They are standard Unicode characters that look like styled letters. I built Fontaly so anyone can type a phrase, preview more than 25 Unicode styles at once, and copy-paste the result into Instagram, WhatsApp, Discord, TikTok, or X without signing up.

Under the hood, a Unicode font generator relies on character mapping tables. The Unicode standard includes a block called Mathematical Alphanumeric Symbols (U+1D400 to U+1D7FF), which was originally added for math notation. It contains separate code points for bold, italic, script, fraktur, double-struck, and monospace variants of Latin letters and digits. When a user types the letter a, the script looks up its offset in a map and swaps it for the matching styled code point.

Not every style comes from a dedicated code block. For effects like strikethrough, underline, or cute decorative text, the generator appends combining diacritical marks (such as U+0336 for a long stroke overlay) right after each base character. Because combining marks attach to the preceding glyph, you can layer them onto almost any letter or number.

Handling edge cases cleanly is important so the output never breaks. Some Unicode math blocks skip specific letters that already existed elsewhere in the standard, such as the script h or fraktur C and R. A reliable mapper has to include explicit overrides for those exceptions and pass through punctuation, spaces, and unsupported characters unchanged instead of outputting missing-glyph boxes.

To keep typing lag at zero, Fontaly is built with Astro and Preact islands. Astro renders the static shell and style guides as plain HTML, while a lightweight Preact island handles the text input, real-time character transformation across all 25+ styles, and one-click clipboard copy. Every keystroke maps characters synchronously in memory with no network requests.

You can test different Unicode mappings and grab styled text for your social profiles on Fontaly.

articles.title: I always wanted lyrics floating over my screen while I work, so I built it
articles.description: I love music. It's on all day while I work: a playlist in the background, code in front of me.  And...
articles.body_html:
I love music. It's on all day while I work: a playlist in the background, code in front of me.

And for a long time I've wished for one thing: the lyrics, right there on my screen, on top of whatever I'm doing. Not in another window I have to switch to. Not in a lyrics tab buried behind my editor. Just floating over my work, word by word, in time with the song, so I can sing along without stopping.

So I finally built it.

mondegreen is a free, open-source lyrics overlay for Windows. Play a song in Spotify or YouTube, and the lyrics float on top of every window. Every word lights up the moment it's sung, and everything moves on the beat, so you feel the song instead of just reading it. And when I only want to listen, Ctrl Alt F turns it into a full-screen lyrics visualizer.

(The name: a "mondegreen" is a misheard lyric, like "'scuse me while I kiss this guy." With the real words on screen, those get fixed too.)

nirajkhetre / mondegreen

Free synced lyrics overlay for Spotify on Windows: word-by-word karaoke lyrics on top of your screen, moving with the beat, plus a full-screen lyrics visualizer.

mondegreen: synced lyrics overlay for Spotify on Windows

Word-by-word lyrics that sing along on top of your screen while you work, move with the beat of the song, and turn into a full-screen music visualizer when you just want to listen.

Website · Wiki · Download · Report a bug

A mondegreen is a misheard lyric: "'Scuse me while I kiss this guy." This app is the fix. It shows you the real words, exactly when they're sung.

Why mondegreen

  • Synced to the word, not just the line. Every word lights up the moment it's sung, from word-timed karaoke lyrics, so you never lose your place.
  • It feels the beat. A beat tracker listens to your speakers and locks onto the tempo, so the lyrics bounce, slam and glow on the beat instead of reacting late.
  • Out of your way. A click-through overlay that floats above every window, hides a…
View on GitHub

Getting lyrics on screen was the easy part. Getting them to land exactly when they're sung, and to move on the beat rather than after it, took most of the work. Here's how each piece works.

1. Knowing exactly where the song is

My first version polled the player's position and drifted. Lyrics were a few hundred milliseconds late, then early, then late.

Windows already knows what's playing: the Global System Media Transport Controls session (the media flyout you see when you press a volume key). No Spotify login, no API key, no Premium. I read it from a tiny PowerShell script that prints a JSON line whenever something changes:

$t = $s.GetTimelineProperties()
$o = [ordered]@{
  app = $s.SourceAppUserModelId; title = $meta.Title; artist = $meta.Artist
  pos = [int]$t.Position.TotalMilliseconds; dur = [int]$t.EndTime.TotalMilliseconds
  at = $t.LastUpdatedTime.ToUnixTimeMilliseconds()
  playing = ($s.GetPlaybackInfo().PlaybackStatus.ToString() -eq 'Playing')
}

The key is LastUpdatedTime. Each position report carries the player's own timestamp for that position. So between reports I don't guess: the position right now is pos + (now − at).

// the player stamps each position report with its own clock (np.at), so between reports we extrapolate exactly;
// small disagreements glide in instead of jumping, seeks snap
function songPos(now) {
  const np = L.np, target = np.playing ? np.pos + (Date.now() - np.at) : np.pos || 0
  const est = shown + (np.playing ? now - shownAt : 0)
  shown = Math.abs(target - est) > 250 ? target : est + (target - est) * 0.06
  shownAt = now
  return shown - (L.S.delay || 0) + (L.S.offsets?.[L.key] || 0)
}

That one change fixed the drift. On real Spotify songs, vocals came in within 20–200 ms of the line starts. For the songs where a lyric file is off, there's a tap-to-sync shortcut that remembers the offset per song.

One thing I tried and rejected: a native SMTC module for Node. Its lastUpdatedTime came back as the query time, not the player's stamp, which breaks exactly this trick.

2. Lighting up every word

Most synced lyrics are timed per line. I wanted every word.

Kugou's KRC format times every syllable. The files are base64, with a 4-byte header, XOR'd with a fixed 16-byte key, then zlib-compressed. Decoding is four lines in Node:

const raw = Buffer.from(d.content, 'base64').subarray(4)
for (let i = 0; i < raw.length; i++) raw[i] ^= KRC_KEY[i % 16]
const lines = parseKrc(zlib.inflateSync(raw).toString('utf8'), c)
return lines.length > 3 ? { source: 'Kugou', kind: 'word', lines } : null

When Kugou has nothing, LRCLIB is the fallback, with line timing; I spread the words across each line by syllable count so they still light up one by one.

The rule that saved me from the most wrong lyrics: both sources must match the track's length (within 3–4 seconds). A live version or an extended mix never gets studio timing. YouTube titles like Artist - Song (Official Video) [4K] get cleaned up before searching, and everything is cached on disk, so a song you've played before shows its lyrics instantly, even offline.

3. Hearing the beat before it lands

Reacting to the beat isn't enough. By the time you detect a kick, it's already over, so anything you animate is late. I wanted the page to know when the next beat lands.

Everything runs in an AudioWorklet on the audio thread, fed by system-audio loopback:

  1. Onset envelope. Split the audio into low, mid and high bands and keep the rises in energy (spectral flux), about 94 frames a second.
  2. Tempo. Autocorrelate the last 8 seconds of that envelope. Peaks are candidate beat periods; a soft preference for ~120 BPM stops it from picking half or double the real tempo: 
const bpm = 60 * fps / L, s = r[L] * Math.exp(-0.5 * (Math.log2(bpm / 120) / 0.8) ** 2)
  1. Hold the grid. The hardest bug: on some songs it kept flipping between half and double the real tempo, and the whole scene jittered. Half, double and 2:3 tempos are the same groove heard differently, so they never reset the grid. A genuinely new tempo has to win four checks in a row: 
else if (![0.5, 2 / 3, 1.5, 2].some(h => Math.abs(ratio / h - 1) < 0.045) && candConf > 0.35) {
  if (this.streak && Math.abs(cand / this.challenger - 1) < 0.04) this.streak++
  else { this.challenger = cand; this.streak = 1 }
  if (this.streak >= 4) { this.period = cand; this.anchor = 0; this.streak = 0 }
}
  1. Phase lock. Find the offset where the last ~4 seconds of onsets pile up, then nudge the grid halfway toward it on each check, like a phase-locked loop with a gain of 0.5.

With that, the grid error on real songs dropped to 0–9 ms. Animations are scheduled for the predicted beat, so they land on it. When there's no steady tempo (intros, ballads), confidence drops and the visuals react to hits instead.

4. What a 144 Hz screen did to my CPU

The first build used CSS animations everywhere. On my laptop's 144 Hz screen, every one of them ran 144 times a second, inside a transparent always-on-top window, which costs a full copy per frame. The overlay sat at up to 127% of a core; the settings window, with its live previews, hit 275%.

The fix: no CSS animations or filters on anything that moves. One loop drives all motion by setting a few CSS variables per word, capped at 60 fps (or 30), sleeping with setTimeout and only then asking for a frame:

// sleep until the next frame is due, then ask for a frame (asking every vsync would wake us 144 times a second)
if (f.paused) timer = setTimeout(() => loop(performance.now()), 100)
else timer = setTimeout(() => { timer = 0; raf = requestAnimationFrame(loop) }, Math.max(0, FRAME - (performance.now() - drawn) - 6))

The overlay dropped to 40–70% of one core while animating, about 6% hidden. Settings went from 275% to about 85%, mostly by letting preview cards animate only under the mouse.

5. Twelve looks and ten full-screen scenes

Since every look reads the same word timings and beat clock, adding looks became fun: a notch that stretches to each line, a split-flap departures board, a ransom-note zine, words that fall and bounce on the beat. There are twelve.

Listen mode (Ctrl Alt F) runs one WebGL2 fragment shader per scene, driven by a monotonic beat counter instead of time, so lasers jump on beats and suns step down per beat. Each scene is coloured from the album art.

My favourite, Late Night Texts, has no image files at all. It's an SVG drawn in code to look like a sketchbook: feTurbulence plus feDisplacementMap wobble every ink line, a noise mask makes them grainy like pencil, and the watercolour washes are blurred, displaced fills with mix-blend-mode: multiply.

<filter id="sk-ink">
  <feTurbulence type="fractalNoise" baseFrequency=".03" numOctaves="2" seed="3" result="n"/>
  <feDisplacementMap in="SourceGraphic" in2="n" scale="3.4" xChannelSelector="R" yChannelSelector="G"/>
</filter>

The guy never moves; the room does. Sound lines leave his headphones on each beat, and the lyrics arrive as a chat on his monitor. The effect lines re-roll their wobble every few frames, which reads as hand-drawn "line boil".

6. Shipping a Windows exe

electron-builder makes the installer and a portable exe. One gotcha to plan for: PowerShell can't read files inside the app.asar archive, so the now-playing script would fail in the packaged app. The fix is to ship the scripts unpacked and point at that folder:

"asarUnpack": ["*.ps1"]

const scripts = __dirname.replace(/app\.asar$/, 'app.asar.unpacked')

What I'd do next

  • Code-sign the exe, so SmartScreen stops warning on first run.
  • Show translation lines (KRC files already carry them).
  • Calibrate Bluetooth latency automatically from the loopback audio.

Try it

It's free and MIT-licensed. Windows 10 or 11, installer or portable exe:

  • Download: https://github.com/nirajkhetre/mondegreen/releases/latest
  • Wiki (deep dives): https://github.com/nirajkhetre/mondegreen/wiki
  • Website: https://nirajkhetre.github.io/mondegreen/

If you work with music on too, I'd love to know what you'd want floating on your screen. Tell me in the comments.

articles.title: How I Built Emojella for One-Tap Emoji Search and Copy in the Browser
articles.description: Finding and copying a few emojis on desktop or mobile often takes more clicks than it should....
articles.body_html:
Finding and copying a few emojis on desktop or mobile often takes more clicks than it should. Standard system pickers close after a single selection or make it awkward to combine multiple emojis into one string. I built Emojella to solve that problem with a fast, browser-based picker where you can search every standard emoji by name or feeling, build a multi-emoji message, adjust the grid size, and set a default skin tone with one tap.

For the architecture, I chose Astro with Svelte islands. The main layout, navigation, and static pages ship as plain HTML and CSS with zero client-side JavaScript overhead. Only the interactive parts, such as the live search bar, category filters, and message builder tray, hydrate as Svelte components. This keeps the initial load small while still giving instant feedback when typing a query or clicking an emoji.

One annoying issue with user-configurable tools is the brief flash of default styles before JavaScript loads. To prevent theme or layout shifts on page load, Emojella runs a small inline script in the document head before the first paint. It reads saved preferences directly from localStorage using keys like ew_theme, ew_size, and ew_tone, then applies the corresponding classes and data attributes to the root element immediately. By the time the browser renders the page, the dark or light theme, grid density, and skin tone are already in place.

Search speed also matters when you have thousands of emoji entries. Instead of hitting a backend API on every keystroke, the dataset is indexed locally in the browser so filtering by name, keyword, or mood happens synchronously in memory. Clicking an emoji copies it straight to the clipboard or appends it to the active message bar, depending on which mode you prefer.

Because people search for emojis in their native language, Emojella supports six locales: English (en), Portuguese (pt), French (fr), Spanish (es), Indonesian (id), and Italian (it). Each localized route has translated metadata and hreflang tags in the head so search engines index the right language version for each region.

If you want a quick way to grab emojis without fighting your operating system picker, try Emojella in your browser.

articles.title: Which JavaScript table library? We built the same table nine times so you don't have to
articles.description: We needed a new JS table library for DataHub's dataset preview: has to show a CSV of anywhere from a...
articles.body_html:
We needed a new JS table library for DataHub's dataset preview: has to show a CSV of anywhere from a hundred rows to half a million.

I went looking for a comparison of table libraries and found lists: a dozen names, a feature matrix, no demos, and often a closing paragraph that just said: "it depends".

So we built a proper comparison:

https://tables.datahub.io

What to use

Here's what we'd use.

Job Use Runner-up
A table on a page (up to a few thousand rows) Plain <table> Observable Inputs
A big grid (up to 500,000 rows, sort and filter built in) AG Grid Community RevoGrid
An editable grid (edit cells, paste ranges) Tabulator RevoGrid

If you are in React and want your own markup and CSS, use TanStack Table with a virtualizer. That is what DataHub does.

What we did

Eight libraries and a plain <table>, on the same UK Land Registry sales data at 1,000 rows, 1,000 rows by 80 columns, 50,000 and 500,000, with the same harness and cell formatter. We measured gzipped bundle size, lines written, render time, scroll FPS, sort at 500,000 rows, text selection, keyboard sort and a small edit test. We also checked 13 features per library: see the compare page.

What we found

Speed doesn't pick a winner. Five grids (Glide, RevoGrid, TanStack, Tabulator, AG Grid) render 500,000 rows in 17 to 233 ms, scroll at 60 fps and sort by price in 0.1 to 0.42 s. Glide has no built-in sort, so its 0.1 s is our own code. Perspective takes 1.9 s and DataTables 8.5 s (its own FAQ says stop at about 50,000 rows).

Four other things separated them.

Text you can find and copy. Every grid except Glide, which is canvas, puts visible cells in the DOM, so Ctrl-F finds them. Only those: a virtualized grid has the rest unmounted. Browser text selection works in the plain table, Observable, Tabulator, TanStack and DataTables. AG Grid blocks it unless you set enableCellTextSelection; Perspective and RevoGrid block it. For a data site this is most of the job.

Weight. From 1 kB for a plain <table> to 332 kB for AG Grid. The chart has the rest.

How it fails. Tabulator's height: "100%", the pattern its docs give for filling a container, renders every row when the parent has no resolved height: 88 seconds at 50,000 rows against 36 ms with a sized parent, and nothing logged. AG Grid, given the same mistake, draws a visibly empty grid.

Whether it's still shipping. Glide Data Grid's last stable release was February 2024 and it is React 16 to 18 only. Our first draft picked it for large data. We reversed that.

The picks

A table on a page: plain <table>. 39 lines, 1 kB, 1,000 rows in about 55 ms. It prints, it copies, dark mode is CSS. But it lays out every row: 2.5 s at 50,000. For sort on click in one call, use Inputs.table(rows) from Observable and keep it under about ten thousand rows.

A big grid: AG Grid Community. 40 lines for sort, filter and virtualization. It is 332 kB as the quick start ships it (272 kB lean). Community is MIT; grouping, pivot, range selection, clipboard and Excel export are Enterprise. Runner-up RevoGrid is the fastest DOM grid we measured at 500,000 rows (62 ms), with clipboard free, if you accept the "RevoGrid" link in the corner.

An editable grid: Tabulator. The test: double-click a price and type, then paste three lines onto a cell. Tabulator passed with options from its own spreadsheet example, all free and MIT. RevoGrid passed with no config. AG Grid Community edits a cell, but paste is Enterprise.

Build your own: TanStack Table with a virtualizer. Headless: it computes rows, sorting and columns and you write every element. Our demo is 150 lines. v9 is a redesign and its docs lag it.

What DataHub will use

TanStack Table with react-virtual, wrapped once as a <DataTable> component in PortalJS. We already ship React, so the table costs 24 kB, not 332, and the preview is text people can Ctrl-F and copy a postcode out of. In exchange we write dataset-wide search, keyboard handling and virtualization ourselves.

Method and caveats

Every figure is the median of five page loads on one M4 laptop in headless Chromium, so treat them as an order of magnitude and re-measure in your own browser. The Tabulator 88 seconds was timed by hand. Agents built and measured the demos under our direction; we chose the verdict. Here are the script and the raw runs.

Try it

All nine are live, with source and the measure buttons:

https://tables.datahub.io

Tell us what we got wrong or missed.

Same treatment for line charts: linecharts.datahub.io.

Contains HM Land Registry data, Crown copyright and database right 2026, Open Government Licence v3.0.

Originally published on the DataHub blog.

articles.title: Why does Circom make me write != the hard way?
articles.description: TL;DR   You'll rebuild last post's "x is not y" circuit in Circom, prove it with snarkjs, and learn...
articles.body_html:
TL;DR

  • You'll rebuild last post's "x is not y" circuit in Circom, prove it with snarkjs, and learn Circom's three arrow operators.
  • Then you'll get a side-by-side Noir vs Circom comparison so you know when to reach for which.

In Post 4, Noir let us write assert(x != y) and move on with our lives. Circom doesn't have that luxury, and that turns out to be a great teacher. Circom makes you see what a circuit really is underneath.

Intuition: Noir is a translator, Circom is a phrasebook

Noir is like a translator: you speak normal-ish code and it figures out the math.

Circom is like a phrasebook: you're allowed to say exactly one kind of sentence, and if your thought doesn't fit that shape, you have to rephrase it yourself.

That sentence shape is:

(something linear) × (something linear) = (something linear)

That's a rank-1 constraint, and a Circom circuit compiles to a list of them, called an R1CS. Every check you want has to be bent into this form. Noir does the bending for you; in Circom, you do it.

The trick for "not equal"

"x ≠ y" isn't a multiplication. So we rephrase:

  • If x ≠ y, then x − y isn't zero, so it has an inverse: some inv with (x − y) × inv = 1.
  • If x = y, then x − y = 0, and 0 × anything = 0, never 1. No inv works.

So "x ≠ y" becomes "there exists an inv such that (x − y) × inv = 1". That is A × B = C. 🎯

(This works because circuits use field arithmetic, where every non-zero number has an inverse. More on that in Post 6.)

Circom's three arrows

Operator Meaning Adds a constraint?
<-- "Compute this value" (a hint for the prover) ❌ No
=== "These must be equal" ✅ Yes
<== Both: compute and constrain ✅ Yes

Burn this table into your brain. Most Circom security bugs live in the gap between <-- and ===.

Hands-on

Full project: code/05-circom-hello.

pragma circom 2.1.6;

// "I know a secret x that is NOT equal to your public y."
template NotEqual() {
    signal input x;          // private by default
    signal input y;          // made public below
    signal inv;

    inv <-- 1 / (x - y);     // hint: computed by the prover, NOT a constraint
    (x - y) * inv === 1;     // the actual constraint
}

component main {public [y]} = NotEqual();

Values in Circom are signals. Just like Noir, inputs are private unless you list them in {public [...]}.

Why can't we write inv <== 1 / (x - y)? Because division isn't allowed in a constraint: it isn't A × B = C. So we compute inv freely with <--, then check it with ===. Compute-then-check is the pattern you'll see everywhere in Circom.

Now the workflow, using snarkjs with the Groth16 proving system:

# 1. compile to R1CS + a WASM witness generator
mkdir -p build
circom not_equal.circom --r1cs --wasm --sym -o build

# 2. compute the witness from input.json: { "x": "1", "y": "2" }
node build/not_equal_js/generate_witness.js build/not_equal_js/not_equal.wasm input.json build/witness.wtns

# 3. trusted setup (phase 1 "powers of tau", phase 2 circuit-specific)
snarkjs powersoftau new bn128 8 build/pot_0.ptau
snarkjs powersoftau contribute build/pot_0.ptau build/pot_1.ptau --name=me -e="random"
snarkjs powersoftau prepare phase2 build/pot_1.ptau build/pot_final.ptau
snarkjs groth16 setup build/not_equal.r1cs build/pot_final.ptau build/key_0.zkey
snarkjs zkey contribute build/key_0.zkey build/key.zkey --name=me -e="more random"
snarkjs zkey export verificationkey build/key.zkey build/vk.json

# 4. prove and verify
snarkjs groth16 prove build/key.zkey build/witness.wtns build/proof.json build/public.json
snarkjs groth16 verify build/vk.json build/public.json build/proof.json

The repo wraps all of this in npm run all.

Yes, step 3 is a lot. That's the trusted setup: Groth16 needs some secret randomness generated once per circuit, and if anyone keeps it they can forge proofs. Here we're the only contributor, which is fine for learning and not fine for production. Post 13 explains why you might accept that deal anyway.

Noir vs Circom: my honest take

Noir Circom
Feels like Rust A hardware description language
!=, if, loops Just write them You rephrase them as constraints
Default backend Barretenberg (UltraHonk) snarkjs (Groth16 / PLONK)
Trusted setup Universal, done once for everyone Per circuit for Groth16
Footgun level Lower (the compiler adds constraints for you) Higher (<-- without ===)
Ecosystem Newer, growing fast Older, huge library (circomlib), lots of audited code

My rule: learn on Noir, read Circom. Noir lets you think about the statement. Circom forces you to understand the constraints, and a huge amount of production ZK code (and audit reports) is written in it.

Gotcha: the <-- that compiled happily

My first draft of this circuit had only one line in the body:

inv <-- 1 / (x - y);

I thought: "if x = y, this divides by zero, so the prover can't make a witness. Done!" It compiled. It proved.

But <-- is only a hint. It runs in the honest prover's witness generator, and a malicious prover doesn't have to use that generator at all. They can put any value in inv. Without (x - y) * inv === 1, there were zero constraints in my circuit, so it would accept x = y (or anything else).

Check yourself: snarkjs r1cs info build/not_equal.r1cs prints the number of constraints. If it says 0, your circuit proves nothing.

Recap

  • Circom circuits compile to R1CS: lots of A × B = C constraints.
  • <-- computes, === constrains, <== does both. A <-- with no matching === is a red flag.
  • Noir is friendlier to write; Circom teaches you what's really happening and dominates existing code.

Next up: we keep bumping into weird facts: no division in constraints, everything has an inverse, == isn't assignment. In Post 6, we finally explain field arithmetic and why you (sort of) can't use if.

Further reading

  • Circom docs: especially "Signals" and "Constraint generation". (though, the domain's down recently)
  • snarkjs README: the full Groth16 and PLONK walkthrough.
  • RareSkills: R1CS: how any computation becomes A × B = C.

Series codebase

All the code from posts in this series will be in this GitHub repo: Zero-Knowledge from zero knowledge

articles.title: Structured Output na prática: do "responda apenas JSON" ao schema validado
articles.description: const resposta = await chamarModelo(   "Classifique este chamado de suporte. Responda apenas...
articles.body_html:
const resposta = await chamarModelo(
  "Classifique este chamado de suporte. Responda apenas JSON."
);

const chamado = JSON.parse(resposta);
await encaminharParaFila(chamado.categoria, chamado.prioridade);

O que pode dar errado aqui?

Se você pensou "o JSON pode vir quebrado", acertou uma parte. Mas o pior caso é outro: o JSON vem perfeito, o JSON.parse passa, e o chamado vai para a fila errada com uma prioridade que não existe.

Este é o segundo artigo da série "IA aplicada ao desenvolvimento de software." No primeiro, sobre RAG, olhamos para o que entra no modelo. Agora vamos olhar para o que sai dele, quando quem vai ler a resposta é o nosso código.

1. "Responda apenas JSON" é um pedido, não um contrato

Quando escrevemos "responda apenas JSON" no prompt, estamos aumentando a chance de receber JSON. Não estamos garantindo nada.

Nenhuma instrução em linguagem natural impede o modelo de:

  • envolver o JSON num bloco de código Markdown;
  • começar com "Claro! Aqui está:";
  • esquecer um campo;
  • inventar um valor fora da lista permitida;
  • devolver "sim" onde esperávamos true;
  • ter a resposta cortada no meio por limite de tokens.

E, mesmo com tudo no formato certo, o conteúdo pode violar uma regra do nosso negócio.

Para o nosso código, a resposta da LLM é uma entrada externa. Deveria passar pelo mesmo cuidado que damos ao body de uma requisição vinda de um usuário.

2. Preparando o exemplo

Vamos classificar chamados de suporte. Cada chamado precisa virar um objeto assim:

{
  "categoria": "pagamento",
  "prioridade": "alta",
  "resumo": "Cliente foi cobrado duas vezes no cartão",
  "precisaHumano": false
}

Para os exemplos rodarem sem chave de API, vamos simular as respostas do modelo. Crie uma pasta e instale o Zod:

mkdir saida-estruturada && cd saida-estruturada
npm init -y
npm install zod

Crie respostas.mjs com sete respostas que um modelo poderia devolver:

export const respostas = [
  // 1. Válida
  '{"categoria":"pagamento","prioridade":"alta","resumo":"Cliente foi cobrado duas vezes no cartão","precisaHumano":false}',

  // 2. Envolvida em bloco de código Markdown
  '```

json\n{"categoria":"acesso","prioridade":"media","resumo":"Usuário não recebe o e-mail de redefinição","precisaHumano":false}\n

```',

  // 3. Texto antes do JSON
  'Claro! Aqui está a classificação:\n{"categoria":"outro","prioridade":"baixa","resumo":"Sugestão de modo escuro no aplicativo","precisaHumano":false}',

  // 4. Campo faltando
  '{"categoria":"acesso","prioridade":"alta","precisaHumano":true}',

  // 5. Valor fora da lista e tipo errado
  '{"categoria":"pagamento","prioridade":"urgente","resumo":"Pagamento recusado sem motivo aparente","precisaHumano":"sim"}',

  // 6. Formato correto, regra de negócio violada
  '{"categoria":"cancelamento","prioridade":"media","resumo":"Cliente quer cancelar o plano anual","precisaHumano":false}',

  // 7. Resposta cortada
  '{"categoria":"pagamento","prioridade":"alta","resumo":"Cliente relata',
];

3. O que o JSON.parse realmente garante

Crie ingenuo.mjs:

import { respostas } from "./respostas.mjs";

respostas.forEach((texto, i) => {
  try {
    const chamado = JSON.parse(texto);
    console.log(`${i + 1}: ok, prioridade ${chamado.prioridade}`);
  } catch (erro) {
    console.log(`${i + 1}: ${erro.name}`);
  }
});

Execute:

node ingenuo.mjs

Saída:

1: ok, prioridade alta
2: SyntaxError
3: SyntaxError
4: ok, prioridade alta
5: ok, prioridade urgente
6: ok, prioridade media
7: SyntaxError

Quatro respostas passaram. Três delas estão erradas:

  • A 4 não tem resumo. O código seguiria com undefined.
  • A 5 tem a prioridade urgente, que não existe no sistema, e precisaHumano como texto. Em JavaScript, "sim" é truthy, então um if (chamado.precisaHumano) funcionaria por acidente, e "não" também seria truthy.
  • A 6 está no formato perfeito, mas manda um cancelamento para atendimento automático.

O JSON.parse garante que o texto é JSON. Não garante que é o JSON que o seu código espera.

4. Um schema como contrato

Vamos escrever o contrato com Zod. Crie schema.mjs:

import { z } from "zod";

export const Chamado = z
  .object({
    categoria: z.enum(["pagamento", "acesso", "cancelamento", "outro"]),
    prioridade: z.enum(["baixa", "media", "alta"]),
    resumo: z.string().min(10).max(280),
    precisaHumano: z.boolean(),
  })
  .refine((c) => c.categoria !== "cancelamento" || c.precisaHumano, {
    message: "Cancelamento sempre precisa de atendimento humano",
    path: ["precisaHumano"],
  });

Esse schema define três níveis de regra:

  • Estrutura: quais campos existem e são obrigatórios.
  • Tipos e valores: prioridade só aceita três valores; precisaHumano precisa ser booleano; resumo tem tamanho mínimo e máximo.
  • Negócio: cancelamento sempre vai para uma pessoa.

Agora, a função que interpreta a resposta. Crie validar.mjs:

import { Chamado } from "./schema.mjs";

function extrairJson(texto) {
  const semCerca = texto
    .trim()
    .replace(/^```

(?:json)?\s*/i, "")
    .replace(/\s*

```$/, "");

  return JSON.parse(semCerca);
}

export function interpretar(texto) {
  let dados;

  try {
    dados = extrairJson(texto);
  } catch {
    return { ok: false, erros: ["json: resposta não é um JSON válido"] };
  }

  const resultado = Chamado.safeParse(dados);

  if (!resultado.success) {
    return {
      ok: false,
      erros: resultado.error.issues.map(
        (issue) => `${issue.path.join(".") || "(raiz)"}: ${issue.code}`
      ),
    };
  }

  return { ok: true, chamado: resultado.data };
}

E um script para testar tudo, testar.mjs:

import { respostas } from "./respostas.mjs";
import { interpretar } from "./validar.mjs";

respostas.forEach((texto, i) => {
  const resultado = interpretar(texto);

  console.log(
    resultado.ok
      ? `${i + 1}: válido (${resultado.chamado.categoria}, ${resultado.chamado.prioridade})`
      : `${i + 1}: inválido -> ${resultado.erros.join(" | ")}`
  );
});

Execute:

node testar.mjs

Saída:

1: válido (pagamento, alta)
2: válido (acesso, media)
3: inválido -> json: resposta não é um JSON válido
4: inválido -> resumo: invalid_type
5: inválido -> prioridade: invalid_value | precisaHumano: invalid_type
6: inválido -> precisaHumano: custom
7: inválido -> json: resposta não é um JSON válido

Usei o code de cada problema em vez da mensagem porque o texto das mensagens pode mudar entre versões do Zod. Os códigos dizem exatamente o que falhou e onde.

Repare em três decisões:

  • A resposta 2 foi aceita. Remover a cerca de Markdown é uma limpeza segura: não muda o conteúdo.
  • A resposta 3 foi rejeitada de propósito. Dava para procurar o primeiro { e o último }, mas isso é uma heurística que pode pegar o trecho errado. Prefiro tratar como falha e deixar a próxima etapa resolver.
  • O schema não preenche nada sozinho. Um prioridade padrão como baixa faria um chamado urgente esperar na fila sem ninguém perceber. Em campo que decide algo importante, valor padrão silencioso é um bug esperando para acontecer.

5. Quando falhar, tentar de novo com contexto

Muitas falhas se resolvem pedindo de novo, desde que o modelo saiba o que deu errado. Crie classificar.mjs:

import { interpretar } from "./validar.mjs";

function montarPrompt(textoDoChamado, errosAnteriores = []) {
  const base = [
    "Classifique o chamado de suporte abaixo.",
    'Responda apenas com um objeto JSON com os campos: categoria ("pagamento" | "acesso" | "cancelamento" | "outro"), prioridade ("baixa" | "media" | "alta"), resumo (texto de 10 a 280 caracteres) e precisaHumano (booleano).',
    "Cancelamentos sempre têm precisaHumano igual a true.",
    `Chamado: ${textoDoChamado}`,
  ];

  if (errosAnteriores.length > 0) {
    base.push(
      `Sua resposta anterior foi rejeitada por estes problemas: ${errosAnteriores.join(", ")}. Corrija e responda novamente.`
    );
  }

  return base.join("\n");
}

export async function classificarChamado(textoDoChamado, chamarModelo, { tentativas = 2 } = {}) {
  let prompt = montarPrompt(textoDoChamado);

  for (let tentativa = 1; tentativa <= tentativas; tentativa++) {
    const resposta = await chamarModelo(prompt);
    const resultado = interpretar(resposta);

    if (resultado.ok) {
      return { status: "classificado", tentativa, chamado: resultado.chamado };
    }

    console.log(`tentativa ${tentativa} falhou: ${resultado.erros.join(", ")}`);
    prompt = montarPrompt(textoDoChamado, resultado.erros);
  }

  return { status: "revisao_manual", motivo: "saída inválida após todas as tentativas" };
}

E o teste com um modelo simulado, demo.mjs:

import { respostas } from "./respostas.mjs";
import { classificarChamado } from "./classificar.mjs";

function modeloSimulado(sequencia) {
  const fila = [...sequencia];
  return async () => fila.shift();
}

console.log("Cenário 1: erra e depois acerta");
const r1 = await classificarChamado(
  "Fui cobrado duas vezes no cartão!",
  modeloSimulado([respostas[4], respostas[0]])
);
console.log(r1);

console.log("\nCenário 2: erra sempre");
const r2 = await classificarChamado(
  "Fui cobrado duas vezes no cartão!",
  modeloSimulado([respostas[6], respostas[6]])
);
console.log(r2);

Execute:

node demo.mjs

Saída:

Cenário 1: erra e depois acerta
tentativa 1 falhou: prioridade: invalid_value, precisaHumano: invalid_type
{
  status: 'classificado',
  tentativa: 2,
  chamado: {
    categoria: 'pagamento',
    prioridade: 'alta',
    resumo: 'Cliente foi cobrado duas vezes no cartão',
    precisaHumano: false
  }
}

Cenário 2: erra sempre
tentativa 1 falhou: json: resposta não é um JSON válido
tentativa 2 falhou: json: resposta não é um JSON válido
{ status: 'revisao_manual', motivo: 'saída inválida após todas as tentativas' }

Dois cuidados com retry:

  • Limite as tentativas. Cada tentativa custa tokens e tempo. Duas ou três costumam bastar; se continua falhando, o problema provavelmente está no prompt, no schema ou na entrada.
  • Repita só a geração. O retry fica antes de qualquer efeito colateral. Se a classificação já disparou um e-mail ou criou um registro, repetir a chamada inteira pode duplicar ações.

6. O fallback também é uma decisão de produto

Quando as tentativas acabam, o código precisa fazer alguma coisa. As opções mais comuns:

Fallback Quando faz sentido
Enviar para revisão humana A decisão importa e existe alguém para revisar
Usar uma regra simples Existe um caminho determinístico aceitável, como palavras-chave
Devolver um erro claro Quem chamou consegue lidar com a falha
Preencher um valor padrão Só quando o valor errado não causa dano

No exemplo, um chamado que a IA não conseguiu classificar vai para uma fila de revisão manual. Ele demora um pouco mais, mas não é encaminhado errado.

7. E o structured output dos provedores?

Os principais provedores oferecem hoje um recurso próprio para isso:

  • A OpenAI oferece Structured Outputs com strict: true, para que a resposta siga o JSON Schema enviado.
  • A Anthropic oferece structured outputs no Claude, com o schema enviado em output_config.format.
  • O Gemini aceita um schema de resposta junto com o tipo application/json.

Nesses recursos, o formato não depende só de o modelo "obedecer" ao prompt: a geração é restringida ao schema. Isso elimina boa parte das falhas que vimos no início, como JSON quebrado, campo faltando ou valor fora do enum.

Vale usar. Mas eles não substituem a validação na aplicação, por quatro motivos:

  1. Exceções previstas. A própria documentação da OpenAI avisa que a garantia não vale quando o modelo recusa o pedido ou quando a resposta é interrompida antes do fim.
  2. Nem todo JSON Schema é suportado. Os provedores aceitam um subconjunto do JSON Schema, e cada um tem suas limitações.
  3. Regras de negócio não cabem no schema. A regra "cancelamento precisa de humano" não tem equivalente em JSON Schema.
  4. Provedor e modelo mudam. Se amanhã você trocar de modelo ou de provedor, a validação na sua aplicação continua protegendo o mesmo contrato.

Dá para manter uma única fonte da verdade: escrever o schema em Zod e gerar o JSON Schema que vai para o provedor. Crie json-schema.mjs:

import { z } from "zod";
import { Chamado } from "./schema.mjs";

console.log(JSON.stringify(z.toJSONSchema(Chamado), null, 2));

Uma saída resumida:

{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "categoria": { "type": "string", "enum": ["pagamento", "acesso", "cancelamento", "outro"] },
    "prioridade": { "type": "string", "enum": ["baixa", "media", "alta"] },
    "resumo": { "type": "string", "minLength": 10, "maxLength": 280 },
    "precisaHumano": { "type": "boolean" }
  },
  "required": ["categoria", "prioridade", "resumo", "precisaHumano"]
}

A saída exata, com campos como $schema e additionalProperties, depende da versão do Zod. E repare no que falta: a regra do cancelamento. O refinamento não tem tradução para JSON Schema, então o provedor nunca vai garanti-la. Ela continua existindo só na validação da sua aplicação.

Juntando tudo:

Camada O que garante O que não garante
Prompt ("responda apenas JSON") Aumenta a chance do formato certo Nada formalmente
Structured output do provedor Formato e tipos dentro do schema, salvo recusa, corte e limitações Regras de negócio e veracidade
Validação na aplicação O contrato que o seu código assume, incluindo regras de negócio Que o conteúdo é verdadeiro
Fallback Um caminho seguro quando o resto falha Que tudo será automatizado

8. Como isso aparece no trabalho?

Saída de IA alimentando outras partes do sistema. Se a classificação decide uma fila, um preço, uma permissão ou um registro no banco, ela precisa do mesmo cuidado que um formulário enviado por um usuário. O JSON.parse seguido de uso direto é o equivalente a salvar o body de uma requisição sem validar.

Limitar o estrago de uma entrada maliciosa. O texto do chamado vem do cliente e pode conter instruções tentando manipular o modelo. Um enum fechado e a validação na aplicação limitam o que essa manipulação consegue produzir: o pior caso vira uma classificação errada dentro das opções válidas, não uma ação inesperada.

Observar as falhas. Registrar quais campos falham, e com que frequência, mostra onde o prompt ou o schema precisam melhorar. Uma taxa de retry subindo depois de trocar de modelo é um sinal que vale acompanhar.

Testar sem chamar o modelo. As respostas simuladas deste artigo funcionam como fixtures. Dá para cobrir a validação, o retry e o fallback com testes rápidos, sem gastar tokens e sem depender de o modelo errar no momento certo.

Formato válido não significa conteúdo correto. Numa aplicação educacional minha, a IA gera relatórios a partir de avaliações dos alunos. Ali, a pergunta mais difícil não é se a resposta tem o formato certo, mas se cada afirmação tem base nas evidências que chegaram ao modelo. Esse é o assunto do artigo sobre RAG: o schema protege o contrato, e o conteúdo ainda precisa de outro tipo de verificação.

Conclusão

No código do começo, o JSON.parse seguido de encaminharParaFila confiava em três coisas ao mesmo tempo: que a resposta seria JSON, que teria o formato esperado e que respeitaria as regras do negócio. O exemplo mostrou que o JSON.parse só cobre a primeira.

O caminho mais robusto combina camadas: um prompt claro, o structured output do provedor quando ele existir, um schema validado na aplicação, retries limitados com o erro como contexto e um fallback pensado como decisão de produto.

Para o seu código, a resposta de uma LLM é uma entrada externa como qualquer outra: precisa de contrato, validação e um plano para quando falhar.

Na sua aplicação, o que acontece hoje quando a IA devolve algo fora do formato esperado?

Referências

  • OpenAI — Introducing Structured Outputs in the API
  • Claude — Structured outputs
  • Gemini API — Structured outputs
  • Zod — documentação
  • RAG: como conectar uma LLM aos dados da sua aplicação, e quando isso faz sentido

articles.title: I Built an Adaptive "Guess My Age" Quiz with Bayesian Inference & Pure Web Audio (No Selfies)
articles.description: Most "guess my age" sites fall into two camps: AI photo scanners that want you to upload a selfie, or...
articles.body_html:
Most "guess my age" sites fall into two camps: AI photo scanners that want you to upload a selfie, or rigid BuzzFeed-style point quizzes where every player gets the exact same 15 questions.
``
I wanted to build something faster, more private, and genuinely fun to play—so I built Guess My Age Quiz: a zero-selfie, adaptive browser game in vanilla JavaScript that estimates your age from everyday habits, childhood media formats, and nostalgia clues.

👉 Try it live (~60 seconds, no signup, no camera): https://guessmyagequiz.com/

Why Not Fixed Point Scoring?

Simple point totals break down fast. If a 22-year-old happens to own vinyl records or a 45-year-old uses TikTok daily, rigid scoring throws the guess way off.

Instead, Guess My Age Quiz treats your age as a probability distribution across 80 discrete ages (6–85) and updates it in real time using Bayesian inference:

  • Gaussian likelihoods per option: Each answer nudges a smooth probability curve (peak, sigma) rather than adding arbitrary points.
  • Shannon entropy & information gain: Before rendering the next question, the quiz calculates which remaining question in the pool maximizes expected entropy reduction—so every tap narrows your likely age window as fast as possible.
  • Coarse-to-fine routing (with rollback): Early questions separate wide generational bands. Once your 10%–90% credible interval tightens to <= 14 years, it switches to finer milestone clues. If a surprising answer strongly contradicts the current estimate, it automatically rolls back to broader cohort clues to double-check.
  • Clean skip handling: Selecting "I don't remember" or "Not applicable" triggers a quick follow-up distinguishing lack of access from never having heard of it, keeping neutral answers from skewing the estimate.

"Most Decisive Clue" Attribution

At the end of the quiz, I didn't want to just print a number and call it a day. To show why the quiz guessed your age, it runs a quick leave-one-out check across your answered clues—removing each answer one by one from the posterior to surface the single choice that shifted your estimated age the most.

It also groups your answers into a decade-by-decade Memory Years Summary so you can see which era your nostalgia anchors cluster around.

Ditching <iframe> for Instant Load

The first version embedded the quiz inside an <iframe>. Clicking Play felt noticeably sluggish because the browser had to fetch a second document, re-parse CSS/JS, fetch the question bank, and sync results back to the parent page via postMessage.

Moving the quiz inline directly onto the landing page—and prefetching the question bank JSON silently while the cover card is displayed—made clicking Play completely instant and eliminated cross-frame state plumbing altogether.

Tactile Retro Sound Effects with Pure Web Audio API

To match the vintage "Editorial Pop-Quiz Dossier" aesthetic without shipping audio files, every sound effect is synthesized on the fly with the Web Audio API (with a Sound On/Off toggle right above the quiz):

  • Per-question click: A 32ms bandpass-filtered white noise burst layered with a 42ms sine pitch-drop (215 Hz -> 92 Hz) for a crisp mechanical card-snap feel.
  • Final dossier reveal: A low-end ink-stamp thump (155 Hz -> 48 Hz) that opens into a low-pass filtered Fmaj9 vintage chord—plus a subtle desk-bell chime if the quiz nails your exact age!

Client-Side Shareable Result Card (HTML5 Canvas)

After a quick post-quiz accuracy check (where you can optionally confirm whether the guess was spot-on or enter your real age), the quiz renders a 900px-wide vertical dossier PNG directly on an offscreen <canvas>—complete with your guessed age stamp, real-age accuracy banner, decade memory bars, and most decisive clue—ready to download or share on X with zero backend image rendering.

Test It Out & Tell Me How Close It Got!

Give Guess My Age Quiz a try and drop a comment below:

  1. How close was the guess to your real age?
  2. What was your "Most Decisive Clue"?
  3. What habit or nostalgia clue do you think is the sharpest age giveaway that I should add next?
